Research on musical instrument classification typically focuses on a limited number of instruments, 
whereas in reality, instruments are diverse and vary from simple to complex. 
Because of this, this study develops a compact network that utilizes a hierarchical structure, 
enabling it to identify a limited number of musical instruments as well as a broader range. 
This proposed model is called HIERA (Hierarchical Instrument Examination for Recognition and Analysis). 
It consists of multiple classification modules, each corresponding to a specific instrument, 
and allows for analysis of the musical instrument in question as well as any other instruments that are not present. 
This approach is unique and has not been previously attempted. 
The proposed method utilizes a pre-trained CNN to extract features from the input audio images, 
and these features are then inputted into a specific classification module that outputs the instrument's name or a signal indicating that the instrument is absent. 
The performance of this method was evaluated using two datasets, 
and experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness both for identifying a limited number of musical instruments and a broader range.

Acquiring specialized knowledge is often necessary for professionals in various fields such as medicine and law, and Knowledge-Seeking Questions (KSAs) are designed to assess an individual's desire to gain new knowledge to answer specific questions. Recent breakthroughs in AI-driven chatbots that simulate human dialogue have highlighted the essential role of KSAs in teaching, testing, and evaluating learners' comprehension of complex subjects, from history to science. Existing evaluation methods for question-answer systems usually involve questions that can be answered with straightforward facts or experiences found in textbooks or encyclopedias. Unfortunately, current approaches fall short when it comes to verifying the system's ability to support learners' efforts to acquire complex knowledge across various disciplines. To address this limitation, we propose the creation of a novel KQA dataset, which will consist of KQA pairs that are grounded in academic research papers, thereby enabling the evaluation of models' capacity to support KSAs across diverse topics and subjects matter.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual eccentric binaries on large orbits. To understand the impact of these sources on PTA data, a crucial step involves comparing various methods used to model the signals emitted by these sources within the PTA framework. In this study, we analyze four distinct waveform models for eccentric binaries and compare their accuracy and computational efficiency when incorporated into PTA simulations, including two established models (Plebański-Lincoln-Thorne and Line-of-Sight), as well as two recently introduced alternatives (ADM4D and GRCholera). Our results indicate that while all four models yield comparable results in the frequency domain, there are significant discrepancies in the time domain, with linear-chain approximations like the ADM4Newton model resulting in notable differences, thus not suitable for PTA signal modeling, unlike the fully consistent GRCholera model, which produces virtually the same results as the exact solution.

We examine the asymptotic behavior of the velocity process in the Asymmetric Exclusion Process, occurring within a finite system of size $n$, under a finite density and polarity configuration. When considered in relation to the configuration, we identify a subsequence of system sizes for which the velocity process converges to an absorbing diffusion process on the interval $[-1,1]$. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of system size on velocity dynamics and provide an analytical method to determine residence time probability distributions for specific intervals. These density-polarity systems can be modeled as random walks with varying boundaries, and our method offers explicit solutions. Notably, our analysis indicates that fast transport phenomena, particularly tunneling, play a crucial role in understanding the complex behavior of the ASEP system.

This study offers an overview of mathematical modelling for infectious disease transmission. It categorises major modelling approaches, including probabilistic and differential equation methods, and discusses various classifications and analysis techniques associated with each. Particular emphasis is placed on understanding epidemic dynamics during current events, with a discussion of model selection, solution methods, parameter estimation, uncertainty assessment, and statistical inference. As a demonstration, two basic models are applied to data from Italian provinces during the most recent SARS-CoV-2 epidemic wave.

The Majorana equation describes fundamental neutral fermions that are their own antiparticles, with applications in theoretical physics and, currently, in quantum computing as qubits. This study examines the general properties of Majorana fermions using a method of linear analysis, with the examination extended to include systems of multiple non-interacting particles. Specific cases, including two particles in a harmonic trap and in a Coulomb field, are studied with attention to energy levels and spatial distribution. The results are compared to those for Majorana fermions in a Gaussian potential and for Dirac particles in a harmonic trap.

Acronyms are extensively used across the World Wide Web to save space and attract attention, but their prevalence creates challenges in Web search, filtering, and extraction. Text containing acronyms is often ambiguous, making it difficult to extract meaningful information without resolving the acronyms. To address this issue, a bottom-up group has developed MadDog, a comprehensive, acronym extraction and resolution tool built on Apache Spark and the Webware for Python framework. MadDog allows users to submit large datasets containing acronyms, which are then extracted using natural language processing techniques. The system provides over ten predefined acronym features that can be customized to suit specific needs, and acronym information is presented through an intuitive, web-based interface. Furthermore, MadDog allows users to create, edit, and manage acronyms, acronym features, and related metadata, acronyms are assigned unique identifiers to facilitate organization, and the system is designed to acconymy resolve names, acronyms, and their meanings.

Converting two-spinor atoms into complex polyatomic molecules via field coupling demands at least two strongly coupled transition dipoles. Successful creation of these molecules demands precise control over the dark-state conditions to avoid unwanted couplings that could cause rapid molecular decay. A newly demonstrated technique achieves this by utilizing a single coupled transition in rubidium-87, transforming a pair of atoms bound by an s-wave into a single molecule with two-body bound states. This process is triggered by an external laser and results in a specific change in the scattering length between the atoms. The transformation occurs within a specific range of angular momentum states and does not interfere with molecules created through radio-frequency induced coupling in other systems or those formed by cold collisions.

Our proposed method, Hierarchical DNA Storage (H-DNS), is a storage system that leverages the potential of synthetic DNA while addressing current limitations.  We developed H-DNS to take full advantage of DNA's high storage capacity and unique error correction properties, and to implement a file system that supports directory and file updates.  We developed a novel update rule and error-correcting code (ECC) to allow for efficient updates without compromising data reliability.  Experimental results demonstrate that H-DNS requires only slightly more energy per bit than traditional DNS, and is up to ten times faster in encoding, and two to three times faster in decoding.  In contrast to current DNS approaches, H-DNS can support the update of storage content, and up to experimental results show energy consumption, runtime, and reliability of the system.

In topological materials, topological invariants play a crucial role in describing the unique properties of electrons near the Fermi level. Recent theoretical and experimental research has revealed another fascinating aspect of topological phenomena - nodal lines in momentum space that give rise to extraordinary behaviors in various non-interacting electron systems. This paper aims to provide a clearer understanding of the mathematical structure of these line nodes, including their classification, and discuss the properties of electrons in the vicinity of these nodal lines. Additionally, we will explore how these nodal lines can be simulated using light and photons in various experiments.

A brain tumor is an abnormal growth inside the skull that can interfere with normal brain function. Brain tumors are classified into three main categories: primary, metastatic, and meningioma. Despite advances in imaging technology, accurately diagnosing and treating brain tumors remains a significant medical challenge. The diagnosis process involves multiple steps, but the treatment plan ultimately relies on accurate image analysis and tumor classification. Researchers have developed machine learning techniques to automate image processing and tumor classification, as manual assessment of images is time-consuming and laborious. In this paper, we present a novel machine learning approach called Multi-task Attention Directed Network, which is designed to simultaneously diagnose, treat, and classify brain tumors in radiology images. Our model utilizes a unique attention mechanism to focus on relevant image features and accurately predict tumor type and location. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Differentiable programming frameworks have gained significant popularity in solving inverse problems over recent years. However, they often encounter scalability issues when dealing with high-dimensional problems due to inefficient gradient computation. Many methods have been proposed to accelerate shadow computation, yet most are limited to specific problems and do not guarantee accurate differentiation. In this work, we introduce an innovative approach that efficiently accelerates shadow computation by leveraging over-complete basis transformation and differentiable optimization, enabling accurate gradient computation in O(k^2) operations per iteration. This method has been particularly effective in large-scale image processing problems, yielding accurate and robust solutions even with significant corruption levels. We have devised three specific recovery problems addressed by our proposed method, which introduces the novel concept of domain transformation to address recovery issues and achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced parameters compared to existing methods.

A deep-deinterlacer that utilizes a single video stream is intensely demanding on computation, particularly when based on 3D convolutional neural networks. In order to reduce this high computation, our proposed method employs two separate 2D network models, with each handling one of the two half-frames. By combining the results, we obtain a complete video frame. To process this in real-time, we have developed two complementary network variants: a prediction model and a decoding model. The prediction model, trained with annotated data, can predict full frames from half-frames in real-time. The results of an experiment show that utilizing the two separate models reduces retrieval time by a factor of 30 compared to using a single 3D convolutional neural network.

Researchers have experimentally verified the average square radius of the neutron distribution for a range of nuclei from ^140Ce to ^142Gd, and in this work the average root-mean-square radius of the neutron distribution is theoretically calculated and compared across multiple relativistic and non-relativistic mean field models. Calculations are performed using a variational method with multiple relativistic and non-relativistic mean field models and it is shown that theory can match experimental data when appropriate parameters are used. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the charge radius in these models is determined by the parameters used for the nucleon-nucleon interaction and these parameters have been constrained by empirical data and theoretical considerations and it is also demonstrated that within the framework of the mean field approximation, average square neutron radii can be calculated efficiently and it is proposed that a more in-depth comparison between relativistic and non-relativistic mean field models be conducted using intrinsic rather than ground-state calculations.

A deep neural network approach is proposed to resolve the barotropic shallow water equations, a set of partial differential equations modeling large-scale barotropic ocean and atmospheric dynamics. The research demonstrates the ability of the developed model to accurately predict barotropic ocean dynamics, even with a limited amount of training data and without incorporating specific boundary conditions relevant to the problem. Furthermore, the team successfully incorporated complex features, such as mesoscale currents and sea floor topography, into the model, and was able to train it using only a short amount of training time. The results indicate that the proposed model can generate highly accurate solutions to the barotropic shallow water equations, even in scenarios with intricate topographies, at a significantly faster rate compared to traditional numerical methods. The team also provides quantitative and qualitative analyses of the proposed model's performance in relation to the original equations and existing numerical methods.

High-dynamic-range photography necessitates capturing images across multiple exposure levels and merging them together, but existing methods demand either images of identical content or smart cameras capable of automatically capturing varied exposures. To circumvent this challenge, we introduce an algorithm capable not only of automatically determining the optimal exposure range but also processing images with different exposures for high-dynamic-range photography. Our algorithm first calculates the ideal exposure range based on smartphone camera characteristics and environmental lighting conditions, then develops a fusion strategy to combine photos at multiple exposure levels without requiring images to be identical. We implemented this algorithm on a standard smartphone and applied it to existing camera applications. The resulting images demonstrate our method's capability to photograph subjects under high-dynamic conditions, such as outdoor scenes with both bright skies and dark trees.

Artificial Neural Networks are now highly effective in addressing complex, real-world problems, particularly those involving vast amounts of data. However, they struggle with certain aspects, such as their tendency to over-rely on data patterns, lack of interpretability, and poor generalizability to new and changing environments. Researchers are proposing the concept of "profound learning" as a potential alternative to traditional shallow learning, drawing parallels to human cognitive processing. This paper reviews the current research on causal methods within profound learning, focusing on their ability to separate cause and effect within data, enhance safety, and adapt to new environments. Despite the promising applications of these methods, there is still significant potential for further development within this emerging field.

Understanding how temperature behaves in catalytic gas-solid fixed beds is crucial for the chemical industry, yet there has been a lack of direct temperature measurement techniques. We utilized real-time magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in combination with specially designed magnetic elements to perform temperature mapping, and observed temperature changes induced by heating gas on non-porous spherical samples at temperatures ranging from 30°C to 60°C. Our findings demonstrate that heating from within the fixed bed results in distinct layers with different temperature arrangements depending on the flow rate, which cannot be accurately predicted by conventional computational models assuming turbulent or Newtonian cooling, indicating the need for further analysis of multiphase heat transfer on external surfaces.

In the context of high-genus compact Riemann surfaces, a statistical analysis of the rational points within the moduli space was conducted by Mirzakhadi and Poonen, revealing the scarcity of such points as genus increases. The examination focused on the cohomology of the compactified moduli space of stable curves, denoted as $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_g$, and its intersection with the Grassmannian, intersecting components, and specific cycles related to $\kappa$, denated as $[\mathcal{M}_g]_d$. The hypotheses that the ratios of the dimensions of the cohomology groups to those of the intersected components or $\kappa$ cycles grow exponentially with genus have significant implications. If true, the hypothesis that the rational points within the non-singular moduli space grow polynomially with genus follows. The relationship between $\left[\mathcal{M}_g\right]_d$ and $\mathcal{K}_d$ has been established for $g$ less than or equal to $3d-9$ and $d$ not equal to 5, with additional values found for higher $g$ values. The relationship between $[\mathcal{M}_g]_d$ and $\mathcal{M}_g$ has been entirely determined for $g$ less than or equal to $3d-9$ and $d$ not equal to 5, with additional values found

This research involves a detailed comparison of the computational performance of various multilevel methods, specifically MLPGE-AMG and having an AMG baseline for solving the complex equations of cardiac mechanics. The studied methods can be divided into two categories: those utilizing a global solver to solve the entire system of equations and a less computationally expensive element-based solver for the majority of the unknown variables or a multilevel approach that solves the equations sequentially from the smallest to the largest scale of the computational domain. The performance of the methods was evaluated on multiple domain sizes and geometries, as well as varying material properties. The results indicate that while the enrichment of basis functions to second-order provides the most significant computational savings, multilevel methods generally do not consistently outperform their element-based counterparts. The ultimate choice of method is highly dependent on the specific application, particularly when considering realistic 3D models.

The asymptotic behavior of large $N$ random matrix ensembles is frequently analyzed by examining their eigenvalue distributions. An alternative approach involves studying independent random matrices, particularly those organized into growth models. This approach has been successful in explaining various phenomena in random matrix theory and relates to statistical physics and probability theory through its connection with non-crossing partition structures. However, there is an unlimited set of tree-like shapes available as $N$ increases, offering the potential to understand higher-order correlations in random matrix theory. This paper aims to fill the gap by investigating an autonomous random matrix model tied to tree-like structures, where the limiting behavior can be described using a combinatorial framework and an explicit equation for a generating function. Our study demonstrates the power of this approach by showing how it can recover the well-understood circular orthogonal ensemble behavior as a particular case.

The pandemic has significantly accelerated the adoption of video-based communication, which overcomes several limitations of text-based communication by conveying information more effectively. However, creating high-quality videos traditionally requires considerable time and expertise, as it involves manually producing multiple multimedia components. This situation has led to a surge of interest in automatic video generation, with significant advancements made in areas such as argumentative article creation, summary-based video making, and transcript-driven audio synthesis. This paper delves into the current state of the art in AI-driven persuasive video generation, examining related subtopics and a key benchmark dataset, ArguVideo, which was specifically designed for this purpose, while also highlighting future research directions in this field.

Every year, billions of dollars are invested in evaluating security systems across various targets, from computer programs to political figures and national infrastructures. These investments in assessment seem counterintuitive given the fundamental principle that an infallible defense is as good as a perfect attack, which can be traced back to von Neumann's concept from 1921. Unfortunately, the current approach to measuring security by examining passed tests is deeply flawed, since many seemingly secure computer programs are successfully hacked every day. Over the past nine decades, the industry has developed an array of methods to measure the false feeling of security in both software and human-driven security systems. However, this metric is rarely applied to assess the vulnerability of computer systems, human factors, or security systems in general. To rectify this oversight, we propose considering the false feeling of security as a new, reliable security metric. To demonstrate the value of this concept, we present three case studies that apply the same logic used to assess the reliability of computer programs to the field of cybersecurity. In doing so, we show that the risk of a security breach is closely related to the number and diversity of defense mechanisms in place, as well as the difficulty of exploiting them. The crucial difference, as opposed to software reliability, is the inability of security systems to anticipate and defend against novel, unexpected attacks. To manipulate microacoustic waves short wavelengths generated above 100 kHz, which are commonly found in piezoelectric MEMS devices, requires a highly refined structural design. However, traditional fabrication techniques struggle to maintain accuracy and intricate details necessary to control these high-frequency waves. Researchers developed a novel approach, combining a microacoustic metagrating design with a two-photon polymerization fabrication technique to control the directional distribution of piezoelectric MEMS ultrasonic transducers operating at 400 kHz. Utilizing a metagrating composed of subwavelength grating units, the researchers were able to control the backward acoustic distribution without compromising the optimal forward performance. By applying this technique, they successfully control the 400 kHz ultrasonic beam using a subwavelength grating with a period of 21.45 μm and achieved an 18-degree electrical specification without any performance decline, demonstrating the potential of this technique in creating complex acoustic devices operating in the 100-kHz bandwidth.

We're dealing with a scenario where the diffusion rates vary randomly in both time and space, leading to unusual, non-Gaussian diffusion patterns that can be described by a fractional diffusion-fick equation with varying coefficients. These patterns are solved using the Fourier-Laplace transformation techniques, and we demonstrate that the resulting solutions align with existing research findings, both analytically and numerically. Our research also introduces new exact solutions to the equation for various scenarios where the diffusion rates change, including a new series expansion method for obtaining these solutions. Additionally, our Monte Carlo simulations, developed from the characteristic function, provide further validation of the results.

A fundamental theory of modern photonics is the electro-magnetic resonance phenomenon.  The precise and reproducible frequencies of optical resonators are the basis for a wide range of applications, including the development of ultra-stable lasers and optical frequency combs.  A comprehensive mathematical model is presented in this paper to describe m-mode optical resonators and their linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions in a systematic and analytical manner.  The developed theory can be applied to various types of optical resonators, providing an analytical method to calculate resonance frequencies and mode volumes for any resonator.  A particular method is demonstrated using a silicon microring resonator to accurately measure non-linear phase shifts at a high level of efficiency.  This paper's findings are of significant value in the field of high-performance photonics by offering a widely applicable design framework for optical components with advanced properties, such as low-power switches and modulators.

We establish precise relationships between stability and performance of control systems and the existence of certain types of value functions that satisfy specific mathematical conditions. These functions correspond to optimal cost problems and are shown to be smooth, adhering to a particular equation known as the Cauchy-Lions equation. Our findings hold for a broader class of linear systems than previously proven, where the control mechanisms are not restricted to bounded values and can have a varying number of dimensions different from the system's output.

A new method is proposed to accurately recover an intricate dynamic system at high Reynolds numbers by transforming a blurred image of a chaotic Rayleigh-B\'enard convection into a highly detailed one using an unsupervised graph convolutional network and a corresponding adversarial loss function.  Our approach leverages the underlying physical patterns inherent in low-Reynolds number flows and demonstrates that the proposed model can successfully increase the complexity of a flow by altering its input resolution.  Experiments show that our method effectively generates images that closely resemble their blurred counterparts across a wide range of Reynolds numbers, outperforming an established reconstruction technique.  The results indicate that our proposed method captures essential characteristics of complex flows and can be utilized to understand and navigate the navigable space of these chaotic systems.

The success of the Wick rotation technique in the path integral framework of quantum field theory has the intriguing implication that the time and spatial components of a momentum vector's behavior should be divergent, the former in the real domain and the latter in the complex plane. Consequently, the spatial components of a particle's momentum may have a theoretical maximum, the so-called cutoff, which could offer insights into the nature of the gravitational force, the vacuum energy density, and the cosmological constant. The proposed approach to introducing this cutoff is supported, and the associated estimation of these physical quantities' magnitudes may prove to be meaningful. The suggested calculation's outcome indicates a value for the wave function's modulus in the real coordinate domain that appears to present the desired characteristics, and whose derivation may reveal a hidden geometric meaning in the squared wave function, the so-called 'density'.

The success of machine learning models for critical life-deciding decisions is heavily dependent on accurate confidence estimation. However, traditional confidence measures are flawed, as they fail to reflect true uncertainty and boundary conditions. This inaccuracy arises mainly from the use of parametric probability distributions, which are limited in their applicability to real-world scenarios. To address this issue, a new energy-based open-world confidence framework has been introduced. This framework generates a loss function that is not constrained by any specific distribution, thus providing more reliable confidence estimation. The proposed method includes novel energy-based losses for both regression and classification tasks, as well as a new confidence optimization strategy. Our results show significant improvements in confidence calibration across various real-world and synthetic datasets. These data demonstrate that our approach yields well-calibrated confidence estimates and accurate predictions beyond the model's known data.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, real-world applications remain rare due to several obstacles, one of which is the prevalence of LFRLMs features that are not typically considered in benchmark tasks such as changing state spaces, transition dynamics, and objectives. Given this challenge, new evaluation frameworks are needed to assess the development of algorithms designed for lifelong learning. This paper introduces L2Ex, an evaluation framework consisting of (1) a comprehensive dataset encompassing over 1,500 synthetic lifelong learning tasks and (2) a standard set of evaluation metrics including convergence rates, performance gains, and negative transfer rates. Finally, an initial analysis is provided to illustrate the utility of this framework and illustrate the potential for future advancements.

Processes that automate business operations within organizations can be efficiently managed and monitored through their declarative nature, a concept highlighted in recent academic research. A notable approach to this is the declarative process model, which emphasizes understanding processes through observation rather than prior specification. This method utilizes observation and data analysis to monitor and investigate processes, ultimately leading to their improvement. This paper delves into the concepts of monitoring and exploration in declarative processes, with a focus on their implementation through probabilistic first-order logic and O-Probabilistic Memos, providing a comprehensive overview of related work and identifying areas for future study.

One-dimensional photonic quasicrystals have been studied for their unique transmission and localizing properties, and recently, we found that adding a periodic component can cause a striking effect called reentrant delocalization. This reentrant delocalization allows light to transition from being localized to propagating and vice versa simply by quasicrystalline design modification, offering potential applications in all-optical switching devices. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that spatial coupling in signal processing can be achieved through this delocalization shift effect, and manipulating the quasicrystalline sequence can optimize transceiver performance in optical communication systems.

Liger, a next-generation wide-field optical imager and spectrometer, is set to debut at the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii in 2022. It is designed to optimize the use of the Keck telescopes for various scientific missions, addressing the demand for wide-field observations. To tackle the expected high data output, Liger features on-board processing, reducing the data rate to 10Gbps per telescope. However, this is complemented by raw data storage of up to 250Gbps per telescope, which can be integrated into the observatory's system upon request. A robust, scalable, and modular software framework is being developed for wide-ranging software applications, as part of the Liger project. This includes the development of new, efficient data-reduction algorithms and the creation of a versatile software interface, as part of the Liger on Keck Observatory (LKO) project, as part of the broader ONC2@Keck initiative.

Optical technology in spatial mode demultiplexing is highly effective in allowing超高分辨率信号 tracking. To achieve this, traditional methods require the number of detectors to be greater than or equal to the number of possible positions being tracked. Our research proposes a novel detection setup that enables two independent methods to separately measure the bi-photon spatial distribution of entangled photons in the Hankel mode. Specifically, we observed the super-resolution feature in the measured spatial distribution. theoretical analysis indicates that the two proposed methods separately measure the intensity and coherence components of the bi-photon spatial distribution. Furthermore, it is shown that these methods are equally efficient in the resolution achievement. Therefore, our research expands the measurement capabilities of the entangled photons in the Hankel mode to their intrinsic resolution.

This paper explores the extensions of algebraic or analytic structures on moduli spaces $M$ to its crossings $M'$, focusing on specific geometric objects like Riemann surfaces. We can define an extension structure on $M'$ based on the intrinsic properties of the objects within the moduli space. The nature of the algebraic or analytic structure on the extended moduli space $M'$ depends on the definitions and properties of these objects.

This paper challenges the conventional view that ecosystems are stable, by analyzing data from a robust mathematical model of an ecosystem with early warning indicators of sudden, large-scale population shifts. A unique method is used to simulate a wide range of subtle shifts and sudden changes, by modifying the model's complexity. Our analysis shows that transients – temporary large fluctuations – can trigger misinterpretations of early warning signs, leading to inaccurate predictions of population stability. A key finding is that the type of transient that occurs has a significant impact on how these warnings are perceived, which can only be fully understood by considering multiple aspects of the ecosystem's dynamics. A specific method is proposed to distinguish between different transient types based on their effect on early warning indicators. This, in turn, can help us differentiate between these transients using only the data available to us. Our research emphasizes the importance of taking temporary fluctuations into account when using early warning indicators, as ignoring them can lead to misjudgments about the stability of an ecosystem and the actions we should take to manage it.

Determining whether stellar mass growth in galaxy ellipticals is primarily halted by the feedback from active supermassive black holes or by the efficient escape of radiation from large supermassive black holes is essential. A comparison of two elliptical galaxies with active supermassive black holes shows that a self-regulating mechanism, mass growth being controlled by the radiation of a large supermassive black holes, may account for the divergence in the relationship between stellar mass growth and star formation rate in high-mass galaxies.

This paper explores the application of multi-task learning to enhance sentiment analysis capabilities beyond available annotated data. Initially, a single-task learning approach was employed, yielding an accuracy of 61%. Subsequently, a multi-task learning approach was implemented, utilizing tasks in four languages and achieving a accuracy of 74%. A notable outcome observed is that, under the multi-task learning approach, the model demonstrated the ability to generalize sentiment analysis capabilities to a task in a fifth language, to which the model had never been explicitly trained.

A well-known problem in computer science is ensuring that multiple processes can access shared data without interfering with each other, and this is commonly addressed using a "fence" variable. However, if the fence's memory gets corrupted, typically a process would need to create a new fence, which can be a time-consuming and resource-intensive task. We have developed an innovative technique for a process to create its own fence and take control of access to shared data without needing assistance from other processes, and we have discovered several significant challenges to this technique. These challenges led us to develop a more effective version of this technique, allowing the process to either keep using the fence if it is still valid or create a new one if it is not. Under specific conditions, we proved that seven processes can achieve this with the help of a limited amount of communication. If the processes have prior knowledge of the system's size, this can be done with just one message; otherwise, it requires up to six messages. We also found a similar technique for a process to downgrade a data access from mutual exclusion to just agreeing that it is valid. This can be achieved with the help of five processes with at most one message. We believe this technique may have potential security applications.

If a finite group G has a subset A with more than two elements such that any element outside of A can be expressed as the product of at least 3 elements from A in all possible orders, then |A| is at least |G|. If A can express every element in G as such a product, it constitutes a basis of size 3 for G. This note provides a new proof of a previously known result's stronger variant (due to H. Cohen), which doesn't require A to be a basis but rather a subset that retains the above-mentioned property, and thus reinforces a known theorem from Freiman and Klyachko that claims if the given condition is met, |A| is at least 2.5 times the size of G. Our new proof utilizes an algorithm to identify a subset of G of a smaller size that meets the given condition, resulting in a variant with a quantitative parameter which leads to the known result when this parameter is set to 1.

This paper examines the measure and topological characteristics of a specific set related to stochastic differential equations, specifically the image of fractional Brownian motion with a fixed drift. By utilizing recent findings by Biagini, Hu, Liu, and Meyer, additional properties of this set will be explored to understand its more in-depth structure. Some of the additional properties to be analyzed include the inner composition properties of this set.

To apply the time-independent variational principle of the Dirac type within the classical and quantum realms, a specific form of the H\'enon-Heiles model was utilized to demonstrate that the method yields the exact equilibrium variables and a specific frequency mode, both oscillating at a distinct rate, through either nonlinear or linear restoration forces. This study extends the H\'enon-Heiles interaction to include a disordered quantum field, showing that the H\'enon-Heiles system, when subjected to this quantum disorder, aligns with the H\'enon-Heiles-Kerman system through a Dirac's variational approach, and can be solved exactly using the H\'enon-Heiles-Kerman equation.

A crucial challenge in predicting which COVID-19 patients will need intensive care is identifying high-risk cases early. This task can be tackled by training machine learning models on chest X-ray images to predict potential severe symptoms. We propose an novel approach called Potential ICU Admission prediction (PICA), a two-step process where a preliminary model flags suspicious X-rays and a second, more complex model analyzes the flagged cases. To succeed, PICA needs two types of training data: clear COVID-19 X-rays and ambiguous, less clear images. An effective strategy is to use simpler models for both steps, pairing a sensitive but not very precise first model with a precise but not very sensitive second model. We designed and built the PICA framework and ran experiments using three well-known chest X-ray datasets. Results show that PICA outperformed a standard single-model approach, achieving significantly better accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 scores.

A key discovery made by Prassidis and Toupsova is that the universal simplicial group in the category of collections is actually a simplicial group. Furthermore, it's proven that this object is a universal simplicial group across all categories of collections, and it equals the 1st homology group of the universal simplicial collection in the category of groups. A significant consequence of this is the equality of the 1st homology group of the universal simplicial group and the universal 1st homology group in the category of collections, which in turn equals the simplicial integer object N^. The demonstration of this lies in the long exact sequence of homology groups arising from the exact sequence of the simplicial integer object N^ and the 0th homology group of the simplicial group.

Despite impressive progress in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), the achievement of a grid-level accuracy remains out of reach. We identify the presence of significant numbers of false detections as a key impediment to further improvement in the task performance. Variations in object boundaries caused by object segmentation inaccuracies and the limitations of current bounding box models result in considerable boundary errors, causing objects to appear disjointed and relationships to overlap other objects. To address this issue, we introduce the Exact Awareness Visual Relationship Detection (ExaAVRD) dataset, consisting of 50,000 accurately annotated scenes from COCO-2014, where relationships are verified to be contained within the objects and not crossing their boundaries. To facilitate the model's learning of such verification, we devise the Boundary-Aware Dual Loss (BADAL), which emphasizes the importance of precise boundary prediction, as well as the containment and separation of objects and relationships. Our experiments reveal that the ExaAVRD dataset enables a significant reduction in false positives, and the proposed BADAL leads to enhanced VRD accuracy and coverage. Furthermore, the integration of ExaAVRD training leads to slight improvements in overall performance.

This study introduces an innovative approach to creating robust action recognition models that excel in low-light conditions with limited training data. Our proposed method, Delta Sampling R-BERT (DS-R-BERT), builds upon the original BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) framework, specifically adapted for video action recognition using the video BERT (vBERT) variant. The vBERT model is part of the Perceiver IO family of models. DS-R-BERT is designed to operate as a compact, restricted model with the capability of learning from significantly fewer training samples compared to its full-sized predecessor. The method employs the "Delta Sampling" technique, which involves presenting the model with a selective sequence of video frames, rather than the entire sequence, to enhance efficiency and reduce computational demands. Experimental results indicate that DS-R-BERT outperforms both traditional and state-of-the-art methods, including the original BERT (vBERT), particularly in low-light scenarios with limited training data.

Content-addressable computers, first envisioned by Von Neumann in 1945 and later by Aiken in 1950, were a ahead of their time idea that got sidelined due to limited fading technology and processing capabilities. These pioneers proposed a innovative design where multiple processors could simultaneously search for specific data within a shared memory unit and update the found information. Despite being a ahead of their time concept, researchers have continuously worked on bringing content-addressable processors to life through various experiments and research projects, ultimately leading to their development on FPGA platforms in recent years. This paper presents an advanced CAP system that integrates two content processors aimed at demonstrating the practical application and potential of this technology.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.94$ within a massive galaxy group, discovering that they are forming stars at relatively low rates compared to their neighbors, which are actively merging. Despite being surrounded by dense dark matter halos that facilitate efficient star formation, the galaxies' central regions exhibit characteristics consistent with a bulge, likely due to star formation in their inner parts. However, overall, the galaxies still maintain a disk-like structure. Further observations in the near-infrared and high-resolution imaging in optical/near-ultraviolet wavelengths will provide more insight into their evolution. These galaxies, residing in heavy dark matter halos, are prime candidates for studying the transition from disk to bulge formation at high redshifts, offering a unique insight into how galaxies evolve under different conditions of mass assembly.

We investigate the universality of the universal texture-zero hypothesis in flavor theory, observing its prevalence in approximately 70 percent of high Bayesian probability regions. The remaining 30 percent exhibits two distinct groups: one where the CKM matrix arises from the product of two texture-zero matrices under the three-zero hypothesis in flavor, and another where no such relationship exists. The textonic MCMC analysis demonstrates that the universal texture-zero hypothesis is not sufficient to account for the observed flavor mixing patterns. The universal texture-zero hypothesis is found to be strongly associated with R-symmetry, yet exhibits insurmountable issues under the framework of textonic theory. The study emphasizes the critical importance of the local probability distribution in the Bayes factor analysis and the necessity of employing the MCMC method to accurately represent the probability distribution within the Bayes factor framework. The study further delves into the relationship between the Bayes factor and MCMC results, as well as the impact of prior parameter choices and their effect on the reliability of MCMC results. The results indicate that the MCMC outcomes are consistent with the Bayes factor findings under comparable prior parameters, and exhibit asymptotic convergence to the probability maximum, where the Bayes factor equals zero, and the log MCMC probability equals one. The equality of the log MCMC probability at the probability maximum and one is established under identical prior parameters. This paper proves the existence and uniqueness of solutions for a boundary value problem arising from a model of a boiling membrane. Additionally, a solution to a related periodic problem is found for a nonlinear薛定谔方程, which has implications for a model of a boiling cable. These findings address an open problem identified by S. A. Possoni and F. Brockate in their 2017 study.

Current techniques for creating programming systems rely on static analysis to evaluate code quality. However, these methods have limitations since they evaluate existing programs rather than guiding the entire code creation process from start to finish. In this research, we investigate using a static analysis tool in conjunction with a neural network to not only assess program quality but also generate programs in conjunction. Specifically, we employ a Markov Decision Process (MPO) framework to train a neural network that can create multiple versions of a program with the same input-output behavior but varying efficiency, while a static analysis tool evaluates their performance. By utilizing this approach, we can achieve code creation across various problem types, including graph transformation, unbounded knapsack problem, and program synthesis, and demonstrate its effectiveness through quantitative and qualitative results. Our findings also highlight the potential for combining static analysis and neural network-based creation systems to generate not only functional programs but also optimized, secure, and maintainable code.

A solar flare that occurred on 7 November 2004 was extremely bright and produced a significant amount of high-energy radiation, including hard X-rays up to several hundred keV, as well as a intense burst of neutrons with a peak value of $1.4\times 10^6$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ on the ground. This observation, made by the China Neutron Monitor located in Lanzhou, China, is the most intense recorded to date. During this event, the neutron flux measured by the monitor exceeded its design threshold by a factor of 40, causing a complete saturation of the detection system. Due to the overwhelming neutron flux, the measurement of electron-positron pairs produced a significant underestimation of the actual number of such particles. By utilizing a correction method developed for this situation, the actual number of such particles is estimated to be 15 times more intense than initially estimated, forming the most intense recorded beam of solar origin to date. This increased intensity may challenge the accuracy of current models predicting particle intensity near Earth's orbit.

In a stationary gravitational field, a stationary sound wave consists of a combination of a wave traveling at the speed of sound and a wave traveling either below or above the speed of sound, depending on the properties of the fluid and the gravitational field. The latter's speed can either remain below or exceed the speed of light, leading to the possibility of radiating gravitational waves. A fluid in a stronger field can produce gravitational waves even when a weaker field cannot. The analysis of a linearized relativistic hydrodynamics confirms the derivation of wave relations first predicted by non-relativistic elastohydrodynamics. The equivalence of gravitational and inertial effects allows these wave relations to be applicable in the vicinity of rotating objects, such as planets, stars, and black holes. The application of these wave relations to a rotating object can result in the generation of centrifugal Coriolis forces and allow for the prediction of the spin of planets, stars, and the spin rate of the Kerr metric's horizon for a fluid filling its interior or extending into the surrounding space.

Observation platforms in quantum mechanics are inherently limited by uncertainty principles, leading to incomplete information about physical systems. This paper proposes a new method for real-time anomaly detection in continuous monitoring of evolving systems using quantum tools, such as qubits. By formulating an error metric based on likelihood and a dynamic threshold that adapts to data density, our approach ensures accurate and timely anomaly identification. Our algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of robustness and efficiency, with a notable improvement of 15% in error rate and 10% speed gain, according to experimental results. By demonstrating the potential of quantum-based anomaly detection, our method could have a significant impact on various applications, such as optimizing communication protocols and enhancing manufacturing processes.

A new government regulation, requiring companies to create backdoors in their encryption systems or face severe financial penalties, has sparked controversy. This requirement poses risks, as it forces companies to verify the integrity of their code with the government, which could potentially introduce spy capabilities into the backdoors. As a means of exploring this issue, researchers conducted a study on four types of backdoor models, including logical, rate-limited, covert channels, and time locks. By analyzing these models in the context of Verifying that the Code is Clean (VCC), a formal specification for code integrity, they discovered that all four models are inherently vulnerable to attack. Consequently, researchers proposed an alternative solution, a formal verification model called Backdoor Detection Specification (BDS), which can identify the presence of any type of backdoor without putting code integrity at risk.

We have created a comprehensive framework for analyzing the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution, which accommodates various real-world factors such as device imperfections, external influences, and malicious attacks. This framework can be utilized to evaluate the security of the protocol and assess its vulnerability to attacks by modeling the process as two sequential measurements in a large-dimensional space. As an illustration, we have applied this framework to develop an optimized attack by ANZ by integrating the efficiency of this attack into our efficiency factor. Furthermore, we have derived an upper bound for the key rate achievable by this attack and compared it to the rate of the ideal MDI-QKD in the presence of device efficiency mismatch. Our efficiency factor also enables investigation of the attack's feasibility given the known ANZ efficiency of qubit measurements. Ultimately, this framework can be employed to simulate the entire security scenario of the protocol, taking into account the efficiency of the ANZ devices, and assess its resistance to various attacks, including the optimized ANZ attack.

Building upon recent breakthroughs in valued constraint satisfaction problems, this paper introduces the first polynomial-time approximate optimization scheme (APX) and the first PTAS for sparse, general-valued problems that are NP-hard to solve exactly. The new PTAS is highly flexible, working for any sparse valuations. As a direct result, significant improvements in approximate solution quality are achieved for specific valuations, including 3SAT with non-uniform clause lengths, the weighted max-3SAT problem, and certain instances of the traveling salesman problem. The approach to these achievements is innovative, combining techniques from low-sparsity-valued constraint satisfaction problems, polynomial method approximation schemes, and valuated homomorphism sparsification.

This study presents a novel Lagrange-Galerkin approach to solving the heat equation, various nonlinear diffusion equations, and their corresponding control problems within a mean field framework. The method is applied to the Fokker-Planck equation, a critical component of a fully coupled mean field system, enabling an approximate solution for the entire setup by integrating the Lagrange-Galerkin scheme with a standard numerical method for the heat equation. The consistency, convergence, and convergence rate of the resulting method are established, while a concrete implementation is demonstrated through one-dimensional examples.

This problem has spurred significant research into comprehending and explaining how DNNs operate, yet existing studies are scattered across the field, leaving a knowledge gap. This survey aims to consolidate current research into comprehending and explaining DNNs, providing a detailed examination of methodological approaches and practical applications, and highlighting areas for future improvement. Stars that are very young and still forming often rotate slowly, a phenomenon that's observed in many young stars forming in groups. Many of these stars also have massive disks surrounding them. According to standard theories of planetary system development, large objects should form quickly within these disks. Such objects would disrupt the stars' rotation by transferring a significant amount of angular momentum to the star through gravitational interactions. This is in contrast to the observed rapid spins of many young stars. Observations of GJ 3337, a star very similar to our own, reveal extremely high rotational speeds but also indicate little interaction with its surrounding disk. Rather than being explained by hidden mechanisms that transfer angular momentum from the disk to the star, this observation suggests that spinning up from small amounts of matter doesn't fully account for the rotation patterns of young stars.

Multimodal news articles that integrate text and visuals have a vast volume on social platforms, requiring users to sort through them quickly. Due to the ease of generating such news with automated tools, the accuracy of the news can be highly misleading. Currently, multimodal false news detection systems rely on hand-crafted features that are often ineffective at identifying emerging detection patterns. In response to this challenge, we propose a groundbreaking, data-driven approach using Neural Process Networks to arrive at an emergent solution for detecting multimodal false news. Our model's architecture enables it to learn the connection between multimodal content and authenticity labels via flexible function approximation, facilitating the rapid classification of newly encountered news without explicit access to the validation data. Experimental evaluations across multiple multimodal datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art techniques, including multimodal embedding methods and attention-based techniques, leading to a significant improvement of over 10% in accurate detection rates.

In modern Internet of Things networks, applications often rely on updating information that is of a critical nature. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in wireless IoT systems, specifically focusing on the refresh process where the source generates fresh information and transmits it to a monitor through a wireless link. The age of information is defined as the time elapsed since the most recent piece of fresh information was received by the monitor, and in this study, we derive the exact distribution of AoI for wireless systems using status updating techniques, for various arrival services and inter-arrival times. The derivation of the distribution of AoI in this study builds on earlier work by extending the approach used in [10] to account for more complex scenarios where an information packet may not always be successfully transmitted due to potential signal loss. The paper also explores the relationship between AoI and other performance metrics, including mean service time, and investigates how changes in these metrics impact the AoI in wireless systems. The paper contributes to the broader field of performance analysis for networks that use AoI as a performance indicator, and our results can be of interest to researchers in this field.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a specific class of set-theoretic type Drinfold twists and provides formulas for their quasi-bialgebra structures, including their coproducts, antipodes, and coassociators. In this research, general assumptions about the set-theoretic type solutions are made to obtain these results for the broadest possible class. Specific examples, such as the quantum torus algebras and quantum matrix algebras, are also analyzed and their quasi-bialgebra properties are derived from previous findings. In this work, generic formulas for the associated quantum algebras are presented and their quantum bialgebra status are demonstrated, while a specific instance of a quantum Hopf algebra is proved.

Recently, Paulus and Zhang identified Golay complementary arrays (GCAs) as a distinct class within the broader context of complementary pairs of arrays. GCAs hold substantial value for specific applications, notably multiway radar systems and code division multiple access systems. This paper delves into various GCA construction techniques by building upon existing methods. Notably, a significant design is introduced, incorporating existing complementary pairs and triples of arrays through direct summation and a modified form of the Kronecker product, known as the HC-matrix product. Several design approaches are developed using the HC-matrix product. These designs, in turn, contribute to the expansion of known GCA parameters in various dimensions and phases.

To perform high-fidelity silicon-based quantum operations, a precise atomic layer of electron confinement is essential.  However, the influence of underlying dopants and silicon valley interference remains difficult to manage.  A novel method is presented here, utilizing an atomically thin barrier within a silicon doped well.  This approach, simulated with the full four-component wavefunction, demonstrates remarkable electron control in a heavily doped silicon layer despite the presence of unsuppressed valley mixing.  Lateral interference between the two silicon valleys can be exploited with a 1% error margin in gate parameters to produce distinct interference patterns in each valley, facilitating efficient swapping of the valley state via a single gate and achieving nearly 99% accuracy in this process even with as much as 15% noise.  Furthermore, the proposed method is robust in this process and largely unaffected by the orientation of the external magnetic field, thus allowing for flexible design of quantum operations and error correction codes.  This technique paves the way for efficient silicon-based quantum computing by enabling precise electron control, effective qubit encoding, and the development of agnostic designs for quantum processors.

Complex systems with interconnected components are ubiquitous and understanding their dynamics is essential for effective management, modeling, and intervention. System component relationships are complex, interdependent, and often changeable. This paper presents a novel, universal framework for modeling dynamic complex systems by leveraging graph neural networks and Bayesian methods. It employs graph stochastic differential equations to capture system component evolution and their interactions, and graph neural ensemble methods to build robust models. The proposed approach is particularly useful in scenarios involving limited data. The framework's components are developed sequentially, and a comprehensive example is used to illustrate the model's capabilities, including its ability to model component lifecycles, time-varying networks, andDYnamic complex systems. The graph neural ensemble method, a first in this context, addresses model overfitting by combining diverse models. It is shown that this method enhances model reliability and accuracy. The framework's success is attributed to its ability to (a) create robust models through graph ensemble methods, (b) incorporate data efficiently through Bayesian inference, and (c) handle complex system dynamics through specialized graph transformations. The framework's applicability is demonstrated in a real-world scenario involving financial market forecasting, where it outperforms existing models. The framework's performance is evaluated through extensive experiments and its code is made available online.

We develop a method to analyze distinguished partitions within the homotopy category of cofibrant suspension diagrams of spaces, which varies in terms of the number of components. This approach yields variations of findings from Cheng and Scherer's research, demonstrating that, for partitions with five or more elements, demonstratable partitions represent the generic behavior in the homotopy category, exhibiting a representability property in the diagram category itself.

Evaluating a brain injury diagnosis model's performance is a complex task due to the limited availability of injured data. To overcome this limitation, injury-aware data augmentation can be employed to balance the distribution of healthy and injured data. In this paper, we develop an improved network called Injury-Aware Progressive Adversarial Auto-Encoder (IAPAAE) for generating realistic images of brain injuries. The generation of injuries is controlled by an injury-aware attention mechanism and an injury synthesis network. A comparison network is used to train the synthesis network by comparing simulated injuries with real injuries. To accurately assess the diagnostic model's performance, we design a constrained evaluation region that only compares injuries within a specific distance of each other. Our experiments on the AISA dataset demonstrate that the evaluation metric within this region closely aligns with the true positive rate in the high-confidence decision region. Moreover, our results indicate that models trained on augmented data consistently outperform those trained on unbalanced data.

The study of robust quantum nonlocality in Heterogeneous Bell Inequalities (HBIs) is advancing, but many questions persist. In this research, we identify a series of unextendible product bases (UPBs) that exhibit robust quantum nonlocality in HBI's framework, demonstrating that algebraic maximal rank (MR) UPBs of odd dimension and maximal diagonalizable (DMR) UPBs possess this property for a broad range of robustness. Local simulations of the robust quantum correlations associated with these two UPB classes are also provided. An analysis of two specific examples, the 9-dimension star UPB and the 16-dimension diagonal UPB, reveals that their respective quantum correlations can be efficiently simulated locally using matchings of size 9 and 16. This work contributes several novel findings to the field of HBI's research, including multiple families of quantum states that exhibit robust quantum nonlocality.

A key challenge in automated task planning for robotic coordination is ensuring complete safe operation in crowded environments with limited space. This paper presents an innovative approach using "astrobots" to complete safe coordination of astrobots in complex environments, as seen in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey V. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of this approach in both computer-simulated and real-world scenarios, confirming its capacity to efficiently complete safe coordination of astrobots. In particular, we demonstrate successful completion of safe coordination of 10 astrobots in an SDSV-like environment.

The OpenStreetMap Project relies on a custom language and interpreter for map object generation, which has been hand-crafted by contributors. However, this custom language suffers from performance inefficiencies that compromise the practicality of its programs. In an effort to rectify this issue, we present an advanced version of the OSMBEef compiler built upon General Purpose Macrose Expansion, demonstrating how it can optimize code through sophisticated macro transformations. Notably, our enhanced compiler achieves a significant reduction of at least 2x in program execution time on at least three instances without incurring the typical performance loss associated with macro expansion.

To maintain the operational efficiency of industrial machinery, monitoring their key components through vibration analysis and extracting relevant features from those signals is essential. This paper presents a unified vibration feature extraction method, focusing on the importance of using consistent data normalization to prevent information loss during the computation of statistical coefficients. Furthermore, to accurately reflect the amplitude information contained in the frequency domain, the method proposes combining spectral entropy calculation with data normalization. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in producing stable and accurate feature values, thereby improving the performance of subsequent fault classification tasks when employing deep learning models without data augmentation, resulting in an average accuracy of 99.59%.

Wreath-type graphs have long been studied due to their rich structural properties, yet much less is known about their twisted counterparts. This paper delves into the autotopism groups of twisted wreath quotient graphs, establishing a collection of graphically regular minimal vertex-transitive autotopism groups of twisted wreath construction. The collection, defined by four conditions, depends on the graph's construction from pairs of isomorphic vertex-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Recent advancements, such as the Group Lasso penalty, have sought to reduce this complexity by reducing the number of active categories. This paper delves into the theoretical and practical aspects of using the Group Lasso for categorical data, focusing on model interpretation. It also explores different post-Lasso strategies to enhance model usability, including reducing model size, ensuring sparsity, and improving fit, while providing an in-depth analysis and relevant examples.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, their tendency to confidently generate incorrect information, a phenomenon known as "model hallucination," remains a significant issue. To address this problem, we propose a framework called SKILL (Structured Knowledge Injection for Large Language Models), which allows models to leverage external knowledge by employing structured information as they would a database. Building upon the concept of Myrells (Makingylls Hallucinations), our approach expands the injection method to support parent-child relationships within a structure and facilitates efficient querying via SQL. Through extensive evaluations of two benchmarks, we found that SKILL successfully reduces hallucinations and enhances factual knowledge performance. Moreover, our results indicate that injecting structured knowledge enables better performance than unrestricted context injection and is comparable to more complex fine-tuning methods like Myrells (Makingylls Hallucinations) and fact augmentation.

This research on vestibular panoramic referencing relies on the minimal solutions concept, which can be divided into two parts: monocular and stereoscopic joining. While binocular vision provides depth information, it lacks relative movement data, making the stereoscopic solution particularly challenging. The problem of stereoscopic joining was addressed using a binocular gravity prior, allowing for the determination of the camera's pose relative to a vertically aligned axis. By representing the panoramic image as a cone in 3D space with two symmetric vertical generators, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the distances of all generators from the gravity vector. A key innovation of this research is the use of robustified costs, allowing for the exclusion of distorted generators caused by objects violating the minimal solution hypothesis. The proposed method was tested on real data, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately estimating the camera's pose relative to the vertical axis even in the presence of distorted generators.
