This paper delves into the characteristics of semigroups of composition operators on BMOA and its extended variant, BMOA_σ, as well as their applications to composition operators semigroups within F(BMOA, BMOA_σ). We define and analyze a class of integral operators, G_φ, with kernel functions mapping BMOA, BMOA_σ, and B(MOCK), B(MOCK_σ) into themselves, then determine the conditions of the parameter φ that ensure operator norm continuity for the semigroup {G_φ^t}.

On social media platforms, the quantity of information being shared online seems to have reached a point of saturation, yet there is insufficient evidence that human understanding of the subject matter is being significantly advanced. In this study, we have taken on the ambitious task of estimating the knowledge base within the domain of physics, in order to assess the efficacy of physics-based research. By adapting an existing methodology for web-page classification to categorize scholarly articles in physics, our findings have been compiled into several key statistics, reflecting the distribution of subject matter within the domain. Analysis of these data revealed several important insights, including the effectiveness of recent research in physics, the impact of prominent individuals and institutions on knowledge advancement, the disparity in publication opportunities between established and emerging journals, and the disparity in contribution recognition between experienced and new individuals in the field.

In this study, we examine an optical wireless communication system that utilizes an relay station to improve security at the physical layer. The system consists of a direct link between the transmitter and receiver, along with an additional relay between them. An eavesdropper intercepts signals from both the transmitter and receiver. Our goal is to maximize the security capacity of this system by optimizing the allocation of subcarriers and power across the wireless transmission. The researcher in this project developed a novel optimization algorithm to efficiently solve this problem, and numerical simulations were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solution.

2D WgQED systems of waveguides arranged in closed loops exhibit the property of topological protection. This creates robust interactions, undisturbed by environmental factors, between localized light modes and nearby atoms. Our research identifies novel configurations of these loop-based waveguide systems that feature factorizable Hamiltonians when the waveguides have gradually changing widths. These systems can demonstrate unique behaviors, including grouped interactions, where some atoms strongly couple to multiple light modes, as well as unidirectional photon emission, where specific atoms emit photons in particular directions, all within a WgQED system using readily available technology.

This paper presents an advanced algorithm for predicting the safe operation of automated vehicles in intersection scenarios, taking into consideration the dynamic behavior of other vehicles and pedestrians. The algorithm utilizes safety constraints based on prediction timelines to ensure the reliable operation of connected automated vehicles in complex traffic environments. A cost function is developed to optimize the speed of a vehicle in relation to traffic signals and surrounding vehicles, utilizing a graph-based optimization approach. The performance of the algorithm is demonstrated through simulations that include multiple scenarios at traffic signalized intersections, showing the ability of the algorithm to manage the safe and efficient operation of automated vehicles in comparison to existing methods.

Text-based games present a challenging platform for AI research, combining realistic virtual environments with natural language interactions and logic. However, their complexity is so vast that it becomes difficult for agents to explore and learn effectively. Our proposal, TextWorldExpress, addresses this issue by significantly enhancing the speed of computer agent exploration in these virtual worlds. Achieving a groundbreaking one million seconds for continuous action simulation, our team uses specialized hardware and customized system programming to surpass the previous limitation of around four thousand seconds. We evaluate text-world games as a multi-layered learning environment consisting of three interconnected components: environment management, image-based reinforcement learning, and text-based decision-making. Our agent successfully learns to play a range of text-based games without prior knowledge, demonstrating a high success rate of 98.8 percent on eight diverse virtual worlds. Notably, our agent also displays a remarkable ability to transfer learned skills from training to previously unseen text-based games.

Deep learning models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been highly effective in processing and analyzing time-series data across a range of applications.  Despite their success, current LSTM implementations often fall short in terms of scalability and efficiency.  As a consequence, developing LSTM algorithms and corresponding hardware that optimize performance and minimize energy consumption remains an open research challenge.  As_lstm_start as video classification, a complex application, is used by researchers to evaluate potential improvements.  In this study, a novel LSTM variant, the Hierarchical LSTM (HLSTM), is introduced to tackle large-scale data sets in a structured, hierarchy-based approach.  The HLSTM's performance is then assessed against the conventional LSTM across multiple hardware platforms, ranging from embedded to field-programable gate array (FPGA) systems.  Results indicate that the HLSTM delivers superior energy efficiency when compared to the CPU-based implementation of the conventional LSTM, and even after accounting for the enhanced hardware of the FPGA system.  Furthermore, a custom HLSTM hardware accelerator is designed and fabricated to maximize energy efficiency.  Experimental evidence suggests that the HLSTM algorithm paired with the hardware accelerator outperforms all previous classifications in terms of energy efficiency across a range of test cases.

In NLP tasks trained on neural networks, obtaining sufficient training data is often challenging. To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed various data augmentation techniques to artificially increase the size of available datasets. Although these techniques have demonstrated significant advantages in certain scenarios, their effectiveness remains controversial due to the lack of comprehensive evaluations across diverse datasets. Our thorough assessment of data augmentation techniques reveals their individual impacts when applied to Neural Machine Translation projects under low-data conditions. Our findings provide guidance on which techniques yield optimal outcomes under specific conditions and highlight the necessity of carefully selecting appropriate augmentation techniques to achieve satisfactory results.

The notion of a charged operator under the conformal generator was introduced, and the properties of these operators were studied within the framework of conformal field theory. A conical surface was defined by the set of charged operators and it was found that the surface exhibits convexity in both free and interacting theories of the type QFT in d-dimensions and 2d CFTs, and the convexity of the surface has the consequence that the set of possible values of the ratio of the conformal dimension and the charge is bounded below, and the magnitude of this lower bound decreases as the central charge increases, and in the limit of a large central charge, this lower bound can be interpreted as supporting the idea of feeble gravity conjecture that scalar fields in two dimensions with a long range interaction should have the magnitude of this interaction be smaller than that of the self-interaction. A particular example of the relationship between the lower bound and the feeble gravity conjecture was also considered and this involved a free scalar field in two dimensions where this lower bound supports the idea of this conjecture in a direct way. A connection of the convexity of the set of charged operators with the principle of the weak gravity conjecture in the same context was speculated.

To advance the precision of quantum simulations for multi-state systems, a new strategy building on Model-Space Quantum Imaginary-Time Evolution has been developed. This approach enables accurate calculation of excited states' properties and transition moments. A key breakthrough is the use of a hybrid Jastrow-PC-PNS wavefunction for joint optimization of electronic correlations and spin structures, allowing for a more detailed understanding of the system's structure across its entire molecular framework. A notable example is the detailed analysis of oxygen molecule's ground and low-lying excited states, where the model-space QFTE method outperformed conventional MP2-based approaches in predicting transition moments.

Given a local ring $(R, \mathfrak m)$ of positive characteristic, we establish a fundamental property of its tight Hilbert polynomial $PH_n$: an $R$-module $M$ possessing finite dimension is $F$-biartinian if and only if it satisfies the condition $(G)$, which stipulates that for sufficiently large $n$, the submodule $\tau_{\mathfrak m^{t_n}}(\tau_{\mathfrak m^\infty} H_{\mathfrak m}(M(\tau_n)))$ has the same dimension as $\tau_{\mathfrak m^{t_n}}(\tau_{\mathfrak m^\infty} H_{\mathfrak m}(M))$ for an appropriate threshold $t_n$. Additionally, we prove that an $R$-module $M$ with a tight Hilbert polynomial $H$ can be constructed from a direct sum of cyclic modules $R/\mathfrak m^{t_n}$ while preserving the dimension condition $(G)$ if and only if $M$ itself is $F$-biartinian. This result can be utilized to determine the tight Hilbert polynomial of an $F$-regular local ring $R$ and its associated modules, and we demonstrate its application in computing the tight Hilbert polynomial of the hyperlog canonical bundle sheaf on a smooth variety over a finite field.

To optimize energy systems through decentralized energy production and consumption, it is crucial to consider secondary benefits from small-scale assets by incorporating them into electricity market mechanisms. However, current market frameworks often fail to account for primary and secondary advantages, underscoring the need for policy interventions to drive the integration of these assets. This paper critiques existing literature on grid connection restrictions, compensation methods, and policy approaches, and proposes a new model that simulates the integration of grid-connected assets within market environments and facilitates policy assessment. The suggested model is capable of calculating optimal asset operation to maximize grid connection benefits, and can be used to evaluate the integration of assets under various market conditions. Additionally, the model is suitable for policy researchers to assess the efficiency and equity of proposed policies. To facilitate the development of custom solutions, the team has created a Python-based implementation of the model using the Open Source Decision Technology (OSDT) framework.

Let K be a field other than with a prime characteristic, and let F(x) = a_x^n + a_{x-1}^n +... + a_0^n be a polynomial of degree n that can be expressed as the sum of degree n monomials. We prove that if polynomial F(x) when plugged in with a prime characteristic a produces a prime value for more than 2n consecutive values of a, then it holds for more than 4n consecutive values of a.

This paper employs the matrix element method to analyze a specific process at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), specifically bhadron collision at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. An extensive study is conducted to evaluate the feasibility of distinguishing between the Standard Model and beyond Standard Model processes involving a pair of Higgs bosons decaying into two bottom quarks and two light gauge bosons in an electron-neutrino final state, with a signal efficiency of 0.0016 and 9 background processes ranked with a confidence level of 90%. Furthermore, the study determines the cross-section for this process to be 3.11 pb, with associated background processes having comparable or lower cross-sections.

We evaluate the impact of extended scalar sectors on precision $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and associated studies, in particular the  $\sigma (γγ \gamma \gamma \to Zh) + \mathcal{L} \to \text{signal}$ and  $pp \to \gamma γ γ γ \to \text{signal}/\bar{\text{signal}}$ processes at future $e^+e^-$ and $pp$ colliders. By including full interference effects between the $\gamma γ γ γ \to \text{SM}$ and $\gamma γ γ γ \to \text{BSM}$ amplitudes in $e^+e^-\to \gamma γ γ γ}$ and unitarity constraints on the couplings in generic two-Higgs doublet models, we derive strict upper limits on the electron form factors at an International Linear Collider. These limits are then used to constrain a wide range of scalar models including type-II 2HDM, $\mu \phi \phi$-type IHDM, and inert 2HDM through their contributions to the electron form factors. Additionally, we explore the potential of $pp \to \gamma γ (γ γ) \to \text{SM Higgs} + \text{jets}/\text{t\bar{t}}}$ at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider for constraining extra scalar sectors. Our analysis shows that precise measurements of $e^

Saturn's upper atmosphere is divided into six alternating zones of warm and cool temperatures that are caused by seasonal temperature changes.  During the summer season in the northern hemisphere, warm temperatures prevail in the equatorial region.  Using observations from the Saturn-based Infrared Radiation Observatory (SOIR) aboard the Venus Encounter of Saturn (Venus Express) spacecraft, researchers tracked the temperature patterns in the polar region over the course of the northern summer.  In the early part of the season, the polar region is quite cold, but as the season progresses, the temperature rises in the area, and distinct temperature patterns emerge.  In the later part of the season, the area experiences quite significant temperature differences, and the differences are quite significant, and as a result, researchers were able to detect the formation of a hexagon in Saturn's northern stratosphere.  The hexagon is encircling the emerging summertime polar vortex, and it is quite a unique phenomenon, and it is also unique because the hexagon is the result of temperature differences, and it is quite a unique phenomenon, and it is also unique because the hexagon is the result of temperature differences.

For a specific set of parameters, including a confining potential and negative energy, we prove that a solution to the time-dependent nonlinear Schrödinger equation does not exist forever in the exterior of a convex obstacle for the Dirichlet boundary condition, provided the nonlinearity grows no faster than cubic. This non-existence result also applies to solutions within a bounded domain under either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions. Our proof relies on constructing an auxiliary equation and applying a compactness alternative. This result represents an improvement over a previously established supercubic solution by Cazenave and Van Den Bank and their collaboration with Tsatsoulis.

Burgos-Gil and Carocca recently introduced the concept of local reduction for varieties defined over a non-zero characteristic ring, demonstrating its utility in lifting these objects to characteristic zero. Local reduction can be viewed as a generalized form of deformation theory. In this note, we introduce the notion of semi-parametric local reduction for families of varieties and demonstrate that families with such properties over a positive-characteristic ring can be lifted to a characteristic-zero ring.

The manner in which V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films are terminated and oxygen-stoichiometric influences their magnetic and electronic characteristics significantly, in particular near the critical point of metal-to-insulator transition (MIT).  High-quality V$_2$O$_3$ single-crystal substrates are employed to grow metal-to-insulator transition preserving ultrathin films via molecular beam epitaxy, utilizing various termination and oxygen stoichiometry conditions are investigated through resistivity, magnetoresistance, and synchrotron X-ray photoemission spectroscopy measurements.  The study reveals that specific surface modifications enable an intrinsic metal-to-insulator transition, whereas other conditions result in an overlying insulator phase resting on an underlying metallic phase with distinct MIT characteristics.  Moreover, particular surface configurations facilitate an unusual intermediate phase characterized by partial metal-to-insulator transition characteristics.  The findings provide valuable insights into the local environment's effect on V$_2$O$_3$'s complex many-body interactions, particularly in proximity to an intrinsic metal-to-insulator transition.

Our study uncovers the complex one-dimensional quantum dynamics governed by the double $U(1)$-symmetry-breaking Gross-Neveu-Becker-Shrfick equation, which we solve to a high degree of accuracy for systems of finite size through an time-evolution-based method. By analyzing these findings, we precisely determine two key aspects: the exact rate at which Bose-Einstein condensation occurs within a confined space, and the specific patterns of quantum state formation in the system's core as well as its surface regions, ultimately revealing a previously unexplored aspect of quantum surface behavior. Furthermore, our work provides a detailed understanding of the long-lasting dynamics of quantum dark solitons that break the system's symmetry.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis includes direct properties of graded bundles and k-fold vector bundles, their morphisms, local coordinates, and spray-based connections. These concepts have been established for degree two, with some aspects of degree three already explored. We discuss the relationship between degree-two sprays and the structure of degree-two graded bundles, highlighting their relevance to the study of torsion-free spray spaces and the degree-two Thomas connection.

Let G be a connected reductive algebraic group defined over the integers in a given rationality domain. For any regular orbital integral defined over this orbit, a specific adjustment factor can be defined. These adjustment factors are products of specific values derived from the algebraic group. It has been proven that these values are invariant under the action of this group. The main result of this research is that the ratio of any two equal-sign orbital integrals generates a specific value and thus equals this adjustment factor. The notion of weak equivalence between algebraic groups is used to prove this equality.

Nuclear reactions produce egressing nucleons that retain significant energy, thereby retaining the ability to form nuclei with novel properties. Traditionally, scientists have relied on kinetic energy spectroscopy to study nucleons, employing this method to research the fundamental properties of nuclear matter. Nonetheless, a majority of the interaction between nucleons is mediated by the strong force, which results in spin and orbital dependent scattering rather than being directly related to particle motion. This research presents a pioneering use of x-ray scattering to retrieve information about the nuclear exit channel, utilizing this method to perform micro-radian resolution experiments with an x-ray free-electron laser. We demonstrate that such experiments can successfully be conducted and possess the capability to identify the properties of the nuclear exit channel.

This research develops a theoretical framework to analyze the performance limitations of quantum error correction circuits, specifically focusing on how noise affects their overall capacity. The study employs tight performance bounds for decoding processes, utilizing an analogy to maximum entropy distribution in order to account for local interactions within quantum circuits. The results of the research indicate the existence of significant, quantifiable constraints on the dissipation and recovery processes in quantum systems, and offer a framework for studying the effects of quantum thermal machines on stabilizing codes. Theoretical implications of the findings are explored, including a connection to quantum systems phase transitions.

Recent theoretical predictions have highlighted topological Insulators as a fascinating area within van der Waals materials, specifically those with large mass gaps. In this context, we present first-principles findings suggesting that monolayers of tellurene, an analog of graphene, can exhibit mass gaps ranging from 420 to 820 meV. These mass gaps can be attributed to its out-of-plane atomic arrangement and intrinsic spin-orbit coupling. Our research indicates that certain functionalized tellurene materials, including -F, -Cl, -OH, and -SH, possess mass gaps exceeding 500 meV, outperforming many previously known 2D topological insulators. Additionally, we predict that certain OH- and SH- functionalized tellurene materials exhibit chemical stability. These discoveries suggest that certain functionalized tellurene materials could be ideal candidates for investigating the properties of 2D topological insulators.

This research introduces a novel hybrid mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow through a fractured medium. The study considers an arbitrary collection of fractures within a bounded two- or three-dimensional domain with smooth boundaries. A specific discretization method is applied to the domain, featuring quadrilateral or triangular elements with a Raviart-Thomas finite element method for velocity approximation and a discontinuous Galerkin method for pressure approximation. The theoretical analysis demonstrates that the method's solution converges optimally in the $H(\text{div};\Omega)$ norm for velocity and in the $L^2$ norm for pressure, with the convergence rate depending on the mesh size for pressure. The method's success is partly attributed to the use of the discrete divergence operator to approximate the permeability matrix. The theoretical findings are complemented by the presentation of the proof, the inclusion of example problems, and graphical results.

A novel device known as a spin switch made from one spiral magnetic layer has been built using advanced materials with intrinsic spin polarization. The spin switch is triggered by a spiral layer's magnetization when a current passing through it experiences the spin-orbit torques generated by the spiral layer. A significant advantage of this spin switch design is its ability to switch between a superconducting and non-superconducting states, making it both energy-efficient and capable of operating at ultra-low temperatures. This characteristic makes the spin switch from a spiral magnetic layer an ideal foundation for developing next-generation, highly responsive superconducting spintronics technologies.

A Bayes factor stands as a unique method inBayesian statistics that enables enthusiasts and frequentist practitioners to compare competing hypotheses, making it an appealing choice for various applications, including confirmatory neuroscience neuroscience imaging analysis. Nevertheless, its significant sensitivity to model parameterization and prior settings complicates its reliable employment in neuroscience. To address this, we present an approach to leverage the distinct sensitivity of Bayes factors to produce statistically robust and reproducible outcomes. We illustrate how predefined workflow parameters can facilitate the utilization of Bayes factors in neuroscience, ensuring its reliable application within the MarsBar and the General Linear Model (GLM) framework in the context of Group-level Neuroscience Imaging (NI) analysis.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "honestly" can convey a wealth of meaning,
conveying essential information for steering the human mind through text.
These discourse indicators are notoriously difficult to grasp,
making them the focus of difficult NLP challenges. They can be context
dependent, vary across cultures and generations, and are frequently used
subtly in text. Due to their ability to convey meaning efficiently,
discourse indicators are also vital for enhancing the ability of
neural networks to comprehend text. Although they are crucial for
effective communication, these markers are often underappreciated and
underutilized in contemporary English writing, especially in academic
settings. To address this issue, a computer system called DiscSense was
created to analyze the use of discourse indicators in text, scoring its
clarity on a scale of 1 to 10 based on the frequency of its use. The
discourse sensitivity of several NLP models was also assessed using this
system, which proved to be a valuable tool in making the discourse
sensitivity of text more measurable and accessible.

Quantum information processing held in the quantum states of a diamond's nitrogen-vacancy center can be processed even at elevated temperatures, despite interaction with the crystal lattice causing rapid state decoherence. Although storing quantum information over longer periods requires cooling or isolation from the lattice, understanding how temperature affects the central transitions of these centers remains crucial. Previous studies provided limited and sometimes conflicting temperature data within a wide range. Our work fills these gaps by obtaining comprehensive high-temperature absorption and fluorescence spectra in both room temperature and high-temperature conditions, up to 450 K, using in-situ spectroscopy. Our findings confirm the stability of the zero-spin state of the centers across these temperatures and the robustness of our methods for obtaining consistent quantum defect pair parameters under elevated heating.

The neocortex is an area of the brain that has not been fully understood, where similar brain areas share common functions. A highly conserved neural network, comprising around 100 types of neurons, can be found in the mouse visual cortex. This complex network is capable of supporting various visual processing tasks through a combination of direct and indirect neural connections. A modeling study presented a novel, highly constrained neural network for the mouse visual cortex that utilizes a local method of performance assessment. This network was presented as a prototype for multiple cortical areas and demonstrates the feasibility of designing functional neural networks via a process reminiscent of evolutionary development and learning.

Investigating an antiferromagnetic $SU(3)$ spin-lattice system on a triangular lattice, we employed a sigma-model approach within the large-$D$ framework to derive the leading-order ($1/D$) corrections to the magnetic susceptibility. Our method involved formulating a suitable sigma-model for each possible magnetization plateau, examining their susceptibility through path-integral renormalization group techniques, and verifying the results using full expansion methods for multiple plateau states. Our main discovery is that most of these states, characterized by specific $SU(3)$ representations, are unstable due to large, divergent $1/D$ corrections, with the exception of two semi-saturated M=4 and M=6 plateaux, which are examined both theoretically and through quantum Monte Carlo calculations.

A new method for the self-consistent field calculation in atoms, molecules, and other systems with arbitrary central potentials has been developed. This method uses a B-spline based atomic orbital set and an adaptive iteration process to efficiently reach a self-consistent state. By combining a flexible atomic orbital basis with a radial potential separation, the method facilitates an easy and effective implementation of the Hartree-Fock-Slater method. It has been demonstrated that an adaptive iteration process, involving the addition of atomic orbitals until convergence is achieved, yields accurate results quickly and accurately for various systems including neutral atoms like Silicon, cationic clusters like Aluminum, and a three-dimensional electron gas. The method outperforms traditional iterative methods by avoiding the convergence issues associated with increasing the number of orbitals, resulting in accurate and reliable results.

To study the explosive transition phenomenon in oscillator systems, we have developed a straightforward criterion that identifies when this transition will occur. By analyzing a broad range of system parameters, we have found that explosive synchronization stems from a zero eigenvalue transverse instability in the system's invariant subspace. Through numerical simulations, we have confirmed that this criterion applies to numerous diverse oscillator models. Specifically, we found that adding random connections between oscillators can generate explosive synchronization if the diagonal elements of the Laplacian matrix satisfy a specific condition. Moreover, we discovered that the strength of interaction required to produce this effect can be significantly lower than previously assumed, making this criterion useful in identifying and characterizing systems exhibiting explosive synchronization behavior.

Nonnegative matrix factorization is a widely used technique in data mining and computer vision applications. Researchers have developed various advanced versions of this technique to enhance its effectiveness, yet they still face challenges of complexity and difficulty in convergence. This paper highlights the issues with convex optimization methods for solving complex factorization problems. It proposes a shift in focus towards analyzing the landscape of optimization problems to find optimal solutions. This shift leads to an interesting discovery - convex optimization techniques can be problematic due to their unnecessary complexity. A global landscape analysis is conducted for a common fixed-rank optimization problem, and the presence of redundant local minima is identified. This analysis prompts reevaluation of approaches that transform difficult problems into simpler ones. The implications for understanding the limitations of convex optimization in fixed-rank problems are discussed, and potential research directions are outlined.

In the context of a bipartite cubic graph, the edge-coloring robustness property implies that under the condition of having no monochromatic subgraphs isomorphic to a specific graph G, the graph itself is 4-colorable by edge. Currently, when G is small, the graph's 4-edge-colorability can be achieved through the coloring method proposed by Vizing in 1964, which concerns maximal matchings. The research study's outcome presents an infinite series of triple-expanding infinite families of graphs that serve as counterexamples to this property, thereby indicating the edge-coloring robustness property as false for certain infinite families of graphs in the domain of bipartite cubic graphs.

Let $q$ be an integer greater than one, and let $\chi$ denote a Dirichlet character modulo $q$. Our research involves proving specific identities related to the novel properties of the Dirichlet $L$-functions at positive even integers, specifically for unprimed or primed summations over primes $p$, the absolute values of the Dirichlet $L$-functions evaluated at such integers, and geometric series formed by primes weighted with $\chi(p)$, where the series are either the sum of the weights or their cumulative totals, and these relationships are also applicable to generalized arithmetic functions.

By studying how particles interact with the energy carried by gravitational waves, we can determine their mass scales. However, an interaction with only two quanta of gravitational waves can result in particles being set into random motions. This can be prevented by considering particles' interaction with the plasma surrounding them, which can be used to set upper limits on their mass. If the particle is lighter than $10^{-17}$ times the energy of the gravitational wave, it will be securely bound. This level of security can be reached in the energy range of $10^{15}$ GeV for a particle interacting with two quanta of a merger event, or $10^{22}$ GeV in the energy range of a high-frequency gravitational wave. This interaction can be implemented by an open string theory, in which case the particle can be connected to a cosmic string, which can emit it.

A microswimmer's flexible, helical tail that swims in a non-newtonian fluid can lead to directional movement as opposed to getting stuck in place, and making the swimmer's tail thinner can make it swim more efficiently in certain types of thick fluids. However, creating such a asymmetric tail-design also causes the swimmer to get stuck in place when using certain types of nonNewtonian fluids.

Through theoretical analysis and computer simulations, it is found that this stalling effect is due to the time-dependent properties of the viscoelastic fluid, which impacts the asymmetric tail more than the symmetric one.

By studying a variety of swimming patterns and fluid properties, a condition is established that predicts when viscoelasticity will have no net effect on the viscerotic asymmetry of the swimmer's tail.

The study also finds an optimal design for the viscerotorically symmetric swimmer that maximizes its forward movement, and observes that these swimmers can take advantage of viscoelastic forces to swim faster than their counterparts in a thin-fluid.

This research paper centers on a critical application of coevolutionary genetic algorithms in a symmetric Cournot game. We employ an algorithm where multiple instances of the algorithm coexist and interact with one another. Our findings reveal that in order to successfully apply this coevolutionary method in a symmetric Cournot game, certain modifications must be made to the underlying algorithm. Specifically, we found that in order to achieve the Nash equilibrium, two key changes must be made: (i) an adjustment to the fitness function and (ii) incorporation of a mechanism that accounts for potential algorithm failures. Notably, these findings can be generalized to other cooperative settings where participants have an incentive to exploit one another.

The growing amount of unstructured data poses significant challenges for enterprises, as basic ODS systems fail to provide meaningful semantic information about hidden relationships within the text. To address this issue, Ontology Enrichment frameworks have been proposed to extract and link valuable information from text to existing ontologies. This paper presents a novel ODS framework called LEAO, fusing state-of-the-art object detection and relation extraction techniques to leverage relationships between ontological entities and text. ODS techniques allow for automatic identification of implicit relationships that may exist between entities and with other entities not explicitly mentioned, and exist elsewhere in the text. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the ODS approach, a competitive ODS model was developed and evaluated on the ORE ontology enrichment dataset, and its performance was quantified through metrics such as ORE-F1, ORE-P, and ORE-R.

Under the influence of a temperature-driven equilibrium, a two-subsystem complete graph model was developed to simulate doped Ising particles that can transition between nonequilibrium states and the equilibrium subsystem. An analytical method yielded precise formulas describing the order parameters for both subsystems when their interaction strength varied. It was demonstrated that the method's results were equivalent to those obtained through Monte Carlo simulations. Notably, a phase transition was found to occur spontaneously at a critical temperature within the equilibrium subsystem, marked by the sudden appearance of a latent heat, which was characterized by an intrinsic nonconvergence property in the associated mean-field free energy. In contrast, the nonequilibrium subsystem exhibited distinct bistable and monostable behavior that could be understood through its effective temperature. The emergence of an isolated point within the order parameter diagram was found to correspond to a sudden change in the system's curvature, which was linked to the Kipness singularity in the local density of states.

Understanding how viruses spread through the air is Crucial for comprehending their transmission and optimizing public health protection. To understand the complex interplay of weather conditions on the dispersion of aerosolized viruses in the environment from a aerial perspective, this study employs numerical simulations of atmospheric physics combined with epidemiology. It is examined how different atmospheric conditions such as fog, clear skies with varying temperatures, and wind affect the dispersion of viruses in the environment using Sars-CoV-2 as an example in typical scenarios of outdoor gatherings under different temperatures, foggy conditions and windy days, respectively. It is found that changes in temperature significantly impact the lifespan of viruses in the air by altering the rate at which they evaporate, impacting public safety in the afternoon more in the cool conditions than in the warm conditions. It is found that the presence of fog slows the spread of viruses, reducing health risks in the presence of humid conditions. It is found that wind aids in the dispersal of viruses in the atmosphere, reducing their concentration on the ground in dry and windy days. It is concluded that the combination of warm conditions, the presence of humidity, the lack of wind and high virus concentrations in the atmosphere are the most favorable conditions for the atmospheric spread of viruses, impacting public health safety in the afternoon on hot and humid days in the late evening.

Causal relationships between inputs and outputs can lead to reliable predictions by models, but this is often unfeasible in many scientific machine learning applications. In such instances, machine learning models are trained to infer functional connections between inputs and outputs based on large datasets, and this can introduce functional models that produce inaccurate uncertainty assessments. As a result, it is crucial to develop methods for evaluating input-dependent reliability in function inputs. In this paper, we systematically examine a wide range of uncertainty measurement techniques applicable to machine learning models. Through extensive numerical simulations and real-world data analysis, we found that several methods failed to accurately evaluate input-dependent reliability. Specifically, our analysis revealed that at least 11 commonly used methods did not meet the necessary criteria for estimating reliable uncertainty measurements. In addition, our data analysis showed that ensemble-based techniques and well-calibrated loss functions outperformed other methods in assessing input-dependent reliability.

This research examines the symbolic and typical behavior of the powers of edge ideals for oriented graphs that have weighted edges. We also explore how this pattern applies to specific classes of weighted oriented hypervertex-partitioned graphs, including complete multipartite graphs and round graphs.

Using a large $N$ expansion, we have developed a non-perturbative understanding of a quantum matrix model based on $O(N^2)$ symmetry, where the classical action is defined by a 'matrix blob' representing specific interactions. This regimen permits us to derive exact equations for the model's singularities and obtain an e^{W} expansion for the free energy. Notably, the model exhibits phase transitions reminiscent of those in type IIA string theory on compactified $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$, even at finite $N$. Furthermore, we have found that the critical points mark the thresholds for the condensation of both bosonic and fermionic particles.

Deep learning systems, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been widely adopted for image classification due to their exceptional accuracy and efficiency. Nonetheless, a significant portion of the research into the robustness of CNNs is centered around software aspects, with relatively little focus on hardware components that contribute to the entire CNN system. This paper addresses this gap by considering the hardware aspects of CNN system robustness in relation to the application of activation range supervision to enhance fault resilience. We propose a method to establish the fault-free correct operation of a CNN system, comprising hardware and software elements, even when subjected to single random memory faults, by defining and bounding the activation range of the network and employing argument range analysis. Additionally, the proposed approach demonstrates activation range supervision can prevent erroneous outputs caused from memory faults, thereby contributing to the development of hardware fault-resilient CNN systems.

The Romanian Ministry of Economy's Monitoring and Support Unit for Private Investment has a monitoring system that ensures private funds directed to companies adhere to contractual terms and Romanian laws. As of 2017, 41 out of 66 privately funded companies in the construction sector owe each other a total of RON 45.8 million in debts, which the monitoring system identifies and reports. This paper presents the Netting Problem, a novel concept we coined to describe netting debts between construction companies. We propose a new method for solving this problem within the specific context of the Romanian Ministry of Economy's needs. Notably, our approach not only addresses the netting issue for these 41 companies but also has the potential to be applied to other construction projects in development.

The Jordanian twist has previously been utilized to modify L-operators and R-matrices belonging to a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, with this work generalizes previous studies by developing a comprehensive framework for Jordanian twists of L-shaped operators and R-matrices within a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. This approach is applied to construct a family of linearly independent twisted coproducts, which in turn enables the development of a comprehensive set of Jordanian-twisted Gaudin Hamiltonians that commute with each other under the influence of twisted Casimir operators. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the derived Gaudin-type algebra possesses an extensive set of commuting operators when combined with its twisted Casimir operators, ultimately facilitating an inductive proof of the shape of its irreducible representations.

We've developed a novel, linguistically universal word representation system, derived from a self-organizing neural network, that automatically constructs a common semantic space without the need for manual alignment or label extraction. Our proposed framework, which we call Cluster-consistent Word Embedding (CoCE), utilizes a cluster-consistent loss function to create an overlapping common semantic space, enabling the subsequent construction of a distinct but related semantic area. A multi-lingual evaluation using eight languages demonstrates that CoCE achieves superior performance, with a 3.62% average improvement in F-score over the state-of-the-art embedding alignment technique (EA-SDP).

This paper outlines the production of various particles such as pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.44 TeV. These particles are important for research into quantum chromodynamics under extreme conditions and the formation of quark-gluon plasma. However, their production mechanisms are complex due to hadron diversity. We have designed an efficient method to identify these particles using the Central Detector in the Compact Muon Solenoid, and demonstrated its effectiveness with data from initial collisions. By comparing our findings to theoretical models such as thermal models and color glass condensate, we can gain deeper understanding of the collision's dynamics.

A large-scale public dataset is commonly used to evaluate the performance of conversation agents, but its reliance assumes that the training and testing annotations are accurate. The discovery of numerous annotation errors in LSTrc2017, when compared to actual user metadata, raises concerns about the performance of current dialogue state tracking models. The assessment of models using this dataset may be skewed due to the discrepancy between model predictions and used annotations versus model evaluated against ground truth metadata. To minimize the impact of this issue, we collected at least 2000 imperfectly annotated conversations that match user metadata testing the hypothesis that models can accurately predict partially labeled data even when trained on a dataset with labeling inaccuracies. The results of our analysis reveal that models are capable of utilizing这些数据 with limited accuracy. The significance of this finding lies in the fact that these data can be used to evaluate the performance of dialogue state tracking models in the presence of labeled noise. The last part of our study explores the potential applications of these data in developing noise-robust models.

In late October 2019, protests in Chile reached a critical point as they spread to various regions and 20 municipalities declared curfews. This study aims to address this issue by first providing an overview of the events that unfolded, and second, offering a mathematical model to track the spatiotemporal progression of demonstrations. The proposed model takes into account population migration between areas and incorporates an integral term to reflect the influence of past behavior on future decisions. Results from the numerical simulations are illustrated through an examination of a particular scenario, and a data-driven inference based on observed patterns in the 2019 protests is presented. The findings suggest that interventions leading to decreases in protest participation can lead to increased participation in subsequent periods, ultimately triggering more intense outbreaks in diverse locations. The model's implications and potential areas for future research are discussed in the conclusion.

Researchers have developed a novel, objective method to create detailed maps of individual stars within galaxies, a process known as star formation rate (SFR) estimation from spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. Nevertheless, this process is hindered by a lack of clarity in reporting, with most studies providing only global SFR estimates rather than detailed maps. In addition, comparing the results of SED fitting to other methods becomes difficult due to differing passbands used in the observations. To address these issues, the authors present a procedure for generating consistent SFR maps from SED fitting, which they apply to a dataset of 12 galaxies spanning a wide range of masses. They further compare the SFR estimates from this procedure to those derived from fitting simple stellar population models to the same data, as well as to estimates from traditional SED fitting using catalog-based data. A crucial discovery emerges from this analysis: there is a significant discrepancy between the results of these approaches on a galaxy-by-galaxy basis, with the new method consistently yielding higher SFR estimates than the catalog-based approach. Moreover, the correlation between the logarithms of the SFR estimates derived from these two methods is only moderate (a correlation coefficient of 0.66). To resolve this, the authors turn to the evaluation of a specific spectral line, the Brackett-$\gamma$ line, with strong theoretical and observational backing, to compare the integrated flux derived from this line with the SFR estimates from these two approaches. We are investigating algebraic varieties and cones within the space $R^n$, specifically a boundary of the SOS cone $\sigma_{2k n}$ with a $2k$-th degree boundary and an underlying hypersurface. This surface can be divided into six distinct parts: (i) a nonconvex section containing a locally convex open area $int(\sigma^\circ_{2k n})$ with an open neighborhood. This open neighborhood allows a $2k$-th root map $\sqrt[2k]{\cdot}$ to be defined and is a local diffeomorphism to an open neighborhood $U$ with a strictly positive identity id. We prove that for $2k\geq4$, the boundary contains strictly positive algebraic hypersurfaces of higher degrees with an interesting collection of smooth strictly positive id's that are not diffeomorphic to each other.

In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish three key constraints: the conservation of lepton number, the unbroken gauge symmetry, and newly defined requirements specific to the FASER$
u$ experiment's design. By examining existing limits from lepton number and gauge symmetry conservation, as well as potential constraints that could be imposed by the FASER$
u$ experiment, we derive particularly stringent limits on certain entries of this matrix, even without assuming unitarity. Notably, the most restrictive current bounds come from the design of the detector itself. We anticipate that future experiments like FASER$
u$ and DUNE $
u$-$\mu$CD will provide much more precise information, potentially revealing deviations from unitarity and informing us about any additional neutrino states.

This paper addresses a challenge in implementing regular expression-based information security tools by developing an algorithm to parse and symbolically analyze constraints involving regular expression concatenation, alternation, and Kleene star operations with a limited depth. The proposed method builds upon existing techniques, extending them to handle the Kleene star where previous methods only dealt with concatenation and alternation, essentially constituting a key component in symbolically analyzing regular expression denial of service (REDoS) vulnerabilities. We designed and implemented an algorithm that parses and solves a specific class of regular expression constraints, allowing for the analysis of binary strings that match certain patterns, e.g., those related to web form validation with the REDoS vulnerability, and determining properties such as the finiteness of the language or the inclusion of specific strings. This work constitutes an initial step in employing symbolic techniques for the automated detection of REDoS vulnerabilities in software containing regular expression operations.

This research proposes a novel approach to two-stage zero-shot visual localization called External Memory Attention Virtual Ization. Given the scarcity of training data in target scenes, traditional learning methods struggle to achieve high accuracy. To address this challenge, our proposed framework allows a network trained on source images to generalize effectively to unseen target locations without any prior exposure to the target dataset. By utilizing an external attention-based memory module, the network can generate more precise visual localization results. We name this approach EMA-VIO. Notably, EMA-VIO allows a network to visualize target scenes that are significantly different from its training data, as long as they share the same geometric structure. We can improve the visual localization accuracy of a network by as much as 200% using EMA-VIO, regardless of whether it's a two-stage or three-stage process.

Yukawa forces, which follow a distance inverse pattern, are commonly observed in condensed matter systems, in contrast to materials called higher-order Weyl semimetals, whose properties are aligned with the linear dispersion seen in ordinary Weyl semimetals. This paper proposes a new class of quantum materials, dubbed square-root higher-order Weyl materials, that exhibit exotic SQSWAY nodes with non-circular cross-sections and SQSWAY dispersion in the energy-momentum relationship. Based on a multi-band model, we demonstrate that these materials can be manipulated using the SQSWAY effect, enabling potential applications in spintronics and quantum information processing.

This study investigates a problem of reconstructing missing data in the equations describing the classical electromagnetic fields. The goal is to complete the equations of Maxwell in a bounded two-dimensional domain, given partial measurements of the electric field and magnetic field over the same area, as well as boundary measurements of the electric field. An inverse problem is formulated based on minimizing the discrepancy between simulated and actual data, given an unknown portion of the missing field data. A quasi-reversibility approach is developed to solve this problem discretely using a combination of finite elements and discrete convolution methods, with an emphasis on numerical verification of the model's effectiveness.

This paper builds on the work of Li and Lin, providing a construction of the parafermion vertex operator algebra associated with the Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$ and its maximal simple ideal, using the method of coset construction from Kac-Moody vertex algebras. Furthermore, the parafermion vertex operator algebra is shown to be rational and have the desired properties in terms of its module structure and fusion categories. This result contributes to a broader understanding of rational vertex operator algebras constructed from Kac-Moody vertex algebras.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Collection (FSC) approach, a novel fedMining variant that enables a teacher network to gather specific data items from a teacher's students. Unlike traditional fedMining approaches, FSC allows students to keep their entries private and only provide access to data that the teacher explicitly requests. The teacher's objective is to create a new model by incorporating a K subset of entries from its student networks, where each student contributes multiple local models but only a requested number of entries are selected from each. The FSC algorithm was implemented and tested on the MNIST dataset with two teacher-student network configurations, where results indicated that it is possible to efficiently collect a teacher's desired data from multiple student networks.

Approximately 10 years ago, the entorhinal cortex's grid cells were first described in detail in a comprehensive review of the rat medial temporal lobe memory systems in the book "The Neurobiology of Memory" by Montarulo and Kesner (2004).

Solar differential rotation significantly accelerates the generation of magnetic fields through the stretching of poloidal field lines by a toroidal component aligned with latitude. This process is a crucial aspect of the solar dynamo and is directly influenced by solar spinning. Investigating solar-type stars with lower rotation rates, a key objective of upcoming missions like Solar-C/A and Don't Worry Be Solar (DWBS), has revealed that some of these stars exhibit magnetic fields that are orders of magnitude stronger than those on the solar surface, yet there is insufficient data to fully understand the magnetic dynamics of such highly magnetized stars. Typically, models assume a direct correlation between solar-type stars' magnetic fields and their rotation rates, classifying them as Rotators with low rotation rates and having weaker magnetic fields or Rotators with strong magnetic fields. To better understand how magnetic fields develop in these stars, researchers utilized a three-component dynamo model to examine the interactions of torsional differential rotation, turbulent shear, and turbulent diffusion in both low and high-rotation stars. Findings from this investigation indicate that turbulent shear's influence is significant in both types of stars, and when taking their rotation rates into account, stars that are not rotating may still generate magnetic fields due to this interaction, while those exhibiting moderate rotation patterns experience enhanced magnetic fields.

Xu Zhang and Xueli Chen have investigated the rank behavior of elliptic curves when extended to certain quartic fields, specifically those with Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$. By analyzing the rank difference between curves that remain isomorphic and those that become isogenous within such extensions, the authors were able to demonstrate an infinite number of instances where the rank difference between isomorphic curves in $S_4$ quartic extensions is odd, and the number of such instances is unbounded. Moreover, they proved an infinite number of cases exist where the rank difference between isomorphic curves in $A_4$ quartic fields is odd, and cases of rank difference being equal to $k$ for $k$ equal to $2$ and $3$ are achievable with curves of global $2$-adic and $3$-adic rank behavior matching their local counterparts respectively.

Quantum systems near critical points can exhibit a dramatic growth in entanglement when driven by an outside force, an increase that is capped by an fundamental inequality known as the quantum null energy condition (QNEC). Using quantum field theories in the holographic duality, we find the exact bound for this saturation of the quantum null energy condition in two scenarios: one involving a rotating charged black hole and another involving a charged black hole subjected to a sudden increase in force. By formulating the saturation of the QNEC in terms of the thermodynamics of the corresponding black hole, we gain deeper insights into this condition. Additionally, we observe a universal behavior in the near-saturation growth rate of mutual information, involving the temperature of the quench and the change in the near-horizon geometry of the holographic BLM information cone.

We investigate the relationship between a system's asymmetry and its ability to return to an initial state, as well as its evolution into orthogonal states, in relation to quantum speed limits set within the Bloch ball. We examine both reversible unitary operations and non-reversible unital maps, discovering that specific states with minimal asymmetry have shorter distinguishability durations and specific relationships with the quantum speed limits for both types of evolution. Our analysis also reveals that certain states with higher asymmetry can still achieve these conditions through a direct connection with the states' asymmetry and monotone values. These findings have potential applications in quantum state engineering and the design of quantum sensors and circuits.

In the context of scientific computing, the development of high-order methods is currently trending, yet their effective implementation demands suitable interpolation tools. This note's primary focus is explaining the evaluation criteria used in this assessment, primarily used to determine the average norm of an interpolation projector on various function spaces. The evaluation metrics used in this assessment are explained in the context of the $L^{\infty}$ norm of cubic Hermite interpolators on triangular elements, where the assessment procedure is clearly illustrated and the potential benefits of this approach are discussed.

Superconducting quantum circuits are the basis for highly sensitive and powerful quantum sensors as well as sensors embedded in resonators. These devices require a precise characterization technique that can accurately measure magnetic fields while minimizing disturbances to the underlying quantum states. Terahertz nanoscopy, when combined with a compact and stable hertzian coil probe, allows researchers to visualize and measure the distribution of electric and magnetic fields within a semiconductor substrate. This technique enables a detailed examination of microwave resonators embedded in indium phosphide, in order to accurately distinguish between the localized field modes of operating modes. Furthermore, it provides an exact scaling of mode shapes in order to determine the coupling coefficient between photons and superconducting qubits. By leveraging the extraordinary spatial and temporal resolution of terahertz nanoscopy, we can accurately characterize and tailor the environment of superconducting quantum processors.

Consider a scheme over a base, we construct a curved K-theory spectrum associated with it. This construction yields the homotopy type of a twisted form of the classical K-theory spectrum over the algebraic geometry over the product of the base with the affine line. If the scheme can be expressed as the graph of a algebraic function over a subdomain of a larger scheme, the integral over this algebraic function transforms the curved K-theory of the subdomain into the classical K-theory of the larger scheme, parameterizing a broad category of such transformations. This concept of curved K-theory is part of a deeper, localized theory that exhibits descent properties and represents the classical K-theory as its ultimate fiber cofibrant form. The curved K-theory spectrum for a scheme over the affine line represents the classical K-theory of that scheme as its most local form. This deeper, localized theory has equivalents in motivic and homotopical homotopy theories that represent the classical K-theory of a scheme as its most local form. The homotopical homotopy theory equivalent of the classical K-theory spectrum over the affine line represents the classical K-theory of that scheme's base, representing a crucial step in understanding the relationship between the algebraic and topological structures of these mathematical objects.

This report delves into the evolution of Venus's atmosphere over various time scales, focusing on planetary formation through to present day and theoretical bare-Venus scenarios. Several processes influencing atmospheric evolution are examined in detail, including volcanism, surface activity, solar stellar evolution, and possible water delivery via accretion and photolysis. The exam also considers atmospheric escape mechanisms such as hydrodynamic and Coulombian escape, as well as NLTE photochemistry. Venus's extreme surface conditions and lack of water are explained, with implications for habitability. The review of photochemistry and escape mechanisms necessitates updates to early-Earth climate models used in the search for biosignatures. The document provides an overview of current knowledge on Venus's atmospheric evolution, including water delivery and its photodissociation, as well as relevant modeling approaches and results.

Ion-based free-space nanofabrication is a promising technique, with glycol being a preferred media due to its high proton yield under UV laser excitation. By utilizing techniques at the molecular glycol droplet level, this study reveals the proton emission mechanisms. High-speed imaging is used to observe the reactions, while spectroscopic analysis provides insights into the generated plasma. The findings indicate that the glycol droplet transforms from a transparent state to an opaque nanosecond plasma, primarily as a result of bond breakdown following the absorption of photons. The emitted protons are mainly released at the droplet surface due to Coulomb explosion, with a minor portion occurring within the droplet due to cascade processes. The proposed analysis enables the examination of complex molecular reactions in real-time.

The representation of many-body systems through matrix product states is a key concept in modern quantum physics, and recent research has established that these states can be equated with deeply nested quantum circuits. Our work builds upon this by demonstrating the decomposition of such circuits into surface-level quantum circuits, consisting of three types of depth-one subcircuits that partition a specific MPSToF network into distinct regions. These regions correspond to separate factorizations of the system's total density matrix, and we认为 this has significant potential for both theoretical analysis and computational efficiency, particularly in calculating thermal properties and time-dependent behavior. Numerical experiments are used to validate the accuracy of these factorizations and assess their precision.

The creation of computer algorithms that can analyze medical images is an established practice, yet developing similar systems for images derived from microscopic examination of tissue is a more complex task due to the immense number of primary images that need to be examined. To tackle this challenge, researchers are developing intelligent systems capable of breaking down large areas into smaller sections for examination, merging these sections into larger contexts, and ultimately combining these hierarchical components to form comprehensive representations of the images. This approach also involves representing the images in a reduced dimensionality to facilitate straightforward comparison and classification. In this study, a novel method is introduced, which employs a specialized classification algorithm to create detailed, hierarchical network representations from images derived from microscopic examination of tissue, and is applied to two distinct problems: distinguishing between healthy tissue and that of patients with lymphoma, and differentiating between tumors that respond well to treatment and those that resist it in patients with breast cancer.

Understanding seismic activity patterns is essential for assessing earthquake risks and investigations into the origins of animal collective behaviors in this research a Bayesian evaluation of the Hawkes process, a model for collective activities, is utilized with the parameters being modeled in a non-linear fashion through splines in a Bayesian framework. This study presents an inference method for the model and examines its effectiveness with synthetic data that includes realistic levels of measurement noise. Additionally, the application of this approach to analyzing the relationship between quakes and acoustic emissions in an experimental setting is demonstrated with data from the MUSE earthquake engineering facility.

In high-accuracy electromagnetic simulation 3D scattering problems, the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is widely utilized to accelerate the calculation of potential interactions among small objects at any given time instance. By representing radiating spherical surfaces with the FMM on a common tree structure, our developed method efficiently computes the time-dependent scattering field outside the objects by preserving angular momentum. Specifically, the transition from Cartesian to spherical coordinates in the FMM domain is accomplished without introducing angular momentum contamination, leading to minimal numerical dispersion and precise sub-wavelength scale phenomena preservation. The implemented algorithm demonstrates significant computational performance improvements, requiring roughly 10 to 100 times less CPU time than conventional FMM approaches in time-dependent simulations.

This work introduces a novel contrastive learning approach to domain-adaptive segmentation tasks with limited labeled data in target domains. By adapting the InfoMax information theory principle, we design a modified objective function that forces the target domain's segmentation results to match those from a source domain, despite domain discrepancies. We evaluate our method on colon and liver segmentation tasks and find it outperforms other techniques in terms of precision, recall, and overall correlation. Our results also demonstrate the flexibility of our approach, which can be applied to various anatomical structures, as long as they share basic characteristics.

Investigating the 1/2+1/2 order and 1.5 order descriptions of supersymmetry transformations in a Wess-Zumino model, we find that while the latter seems to indicate a local formulation of supersymmetry, it actually yields incorrect BRS transformation rules. Our derived BRS transformations for 1.5 order variables differ from those obtained using standard methods, and when applied, result in non-conserved charges. Nonetheless, despite our findings regarding 1.5 order descriptions, we also explore the possibility of a 1.5 order formalism for auxiliary fields within non-gravitational superQFT, and confirm that such a framework exists, is consistent, and preserves the equivalence of quantum mechanical calculations to their 1.5 order counterparts.

Youthful stars that still have their surrounding hydrogen clouds are critical for researchers to understand the processes of hydrogen clouds and stellar polarization. However, studying this polarization is complicated due to the faintness of visible light. To address this challenge, we developed a novel technique to alter and amplify the polarization of highly intense laser pulses when they pass through the hydrogen clouds. By adjusting the magnetic field within the gas targets, we were able to significantly enhance the polarization of the pulses, achieving a 90% polarization rate at 2 PW or higher intensities. This adjustment of polarization can be applied to various fields including quantum plasma studies, advanced imaging techniques, and the emulation of magnetic fields within astrophysical environments.

By analyzing recent data from Belle II, we studied charged tau meson decays to electromagnetic bosons and final states containing hadronic pairs, which allowed us to place stringent limits on the tau lepton's dipole moment. At current settings of confidence interval and lepton flavor universality, we found combined constraints on the real and imaginary components of the tau lepton's dimension-5 operator coefficient, effectively translating to upper bounds on its electric dipole moment. These bounds are so precise that they exceed previous limits by nearly three orders of magnitude, highlighting the potential of the Belle II dataset to reveal new physics beyond the Standard Model, even at its earliest stages.

We confirm that decoding capability of the SyRamp decoder surpasses the expected limit for rank metric code balls, with further clarification, and identify a mistake bound applicable to codes operating under the rank metric, with output, and demonstrate that generic and minimum distance decoding methods function effectively under this constraint, or can be modified to comply, with the rank metric defined in this context being the additional non-zero components required in a difference matrix between two matrices of the same genus.

Building upon the established light-cone operator product expansion (LC-OPE) framework, which simplifies correlation functions by reducing their order by the number of external operators, additional reductions in higher-point functions are anticipated in conformal field theories. In our analysis, we delve into the nature of these anticipated reductions in the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ critical 3D Ising model, with a particular emphasis on the reductions in four- and five-point functions involving primary Heisenberg spin operators. By calculating LC-OPE data and standard OPE data for four- and five-point functions, we identify reduced configurations in these functions and examine the characteristics of the corresponding OPE coefficients in these configurations. Notably, we discover reduced configurations that correspond to spinning OPE blocks in four-point functions in even sectors and in three-point functions mixing even and odd sectors. Moreover, the study of these coefficients raises intriguing questions regarding the existence of a discrete spinning Kac table in the Heisenberg CFT$_2$.

A significant obstacle in analyzing Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations is the reduction of information content and distortion of correlation patterns caused by large-scale structure (LSS) gravitational lensing. Researchers are motivated to develop methods for reconstructing the degraded map and accurately measuring the resulting correlated noise. A novel approach utilizing neural networks is presented, which demonstrates an improvement in correlation pattern recovery and correlated noise reduction. This approach yields a reduction in RMS errors that is 10% lower across a range of scales from 10 angular minutes to 0.1 degrees, and exhibits superior performance at the multipole scale of interest for CMB large-scale polarization power spectrum analysis, when compared to traditional methods. A key consideration in evaluating the performance of this approach is its ability to measure the CMB power spectrum in the presence of primordial tensor perturbations, which hold the potential to unravel the nature of dark energy.

In 1991, Gelfand and MacPherson established a recursive method for determining the Pontrjagin classes of any manifold, based on the combinatorial structure of its underlying point cloud. Building upon this work, we generalize their approach to define higher-degree invariant differential forms on any manifold, derived from its geometric structure. We then demonstrate how these forms correspond to the Pontrjagin forms introduced by Atiyah and Singer in their work on the Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch theorem for elliptic operators, established in 1965.

We investigate SN 2020jfo, a Type II-plateau supernova, which exploded in NGC 4590, a spiral galaxy, on August 14, 2020. Initially observed at a visual magnitude of 18.5, it showed visual and near-infrared features typical of Type II events around maximum brightness. However, SN 2020jfo stood out due to an unusual spectral feature at 6150 \AA, likely caused by highly ionized oxygen III. This feature, combined with its visual and near-infrared properties, points to significant mass loss from the progenitor through a dense circumstellar medium. Further analysis of the spectral data in the ultraviolet revealed extensive UV mass loss. Additionally, SN 2020jfo exhibited a shorter-than-average plateau duration and an unusually bright luminosity during this period. This correlation between short plateau and high luminosity during that period is often associated with super-powered Type II events, although no such events have been confirmed for 2020jfo at peak brightness.

To address the lack of efficient wide-field X-ray imaging techniques with good spatial resolution, novel concepts like lobster-eye optics are being studied. Although previous designs using lobster-eye optics in X-ray lenses and mirrors have shown potential in detecting extragalactic sources like supernovae, they suffer from significant disadvantages in power consumption and cost when employed in wide-field scanners. A new design integrating multiple types of lobster-eye optics based on capillary lenses could lead to enhanced imaging performance and a more compact, cost-effective design, thus overcoming the limitations of this technology when operating in the X-ray spectrum for wide-field applications. Furthermore, the implications of this design for wide-field X-ray monitoring systems, particularly in detecting transient sources, are explored.

In a $C^{1,1}$ domain within Euclidean space, we define two novel concepts: partial uniform ellipticity and level set partial uniform ellipticity for $C^2$ functions that adhere to second-order partial differential equations. Partial uniform ellipticity is part uniform in its coefficients and derivatives, with its effects limited to their boundary. We demonstrate that these two concepts can be utilized to employ the method of moving planes at a rigorous mathematical level. Moreover, we can utilize the level set partial uniform ellipticity in a similar manner to the method of moving spheres. Both of these methods lead to symmetry outcomes, specifically the level set conformal symmetry for non-degenerate solutions of elliptic equations.

This paper builds on a recent discovery by K. Bhattacharjee and S. S. Bhattacharjee, who proposed the existence of a cosmic speed field that could account for dark matter's behavior. A neural network model was trained on a collection of 10^6 Navarro-Frenk-White dark matter halo simulations to determine the halos' concentration parameters and overconvergence parameters. The results showed that the concentration parameter could be accurately predicted by the speed field alone, in accordance with recent theoretical predictions, whereas conventional models required a combination of density and speed field to achieve the same accuracy. When testing the accuracy of the minimum speed field model against the full four-parameter model, it was surprising to find nearly the same level of accuracy, suggesting that the cosmic speed field may hold the key to understanding the distribution of dark matter in the universe.

In this research, a novel method called Semi-Supervised Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (SCNMF) is introduced for automatic musical keyboard transcription. Unlike traditional SCNMF, our method accounts for neighboring information and neighboring errors in the "target" spectrum image, effectively addressing local errors. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Semi-Supervised Convolutive NMF (SCNMF) outperforms the existing SCNMF and other baseline methods in accuracy when applied to musical keyboard transcription.

A new, coordinate-adaptive formulation has been developed to simulate the evolution of rotating stars within the framework of General Relativity. This approach treats the star as comprising multiple co-rotating fluid elements and utilizes a 3+1 decomposition, representing each star slice with a discrete metric, connection variables, and matter content. Notably, this method preserves the symmetry across the star and eliminates the need to explicitly model the internal angular velocity profile. Through the use of adaptive coordinates and a topologically simple 3-torus, we eliminate distortions caused by rotating frame effects and frame dragging. A specific example is provided where we demonstrate the maintenance of angular momentum and angular velocity profile over time in a steady-state star simulation. Our code is currently under test for stability and convergence, and a preview of our results is available for non-rotating stars using first and second-order methods.

A key challenge in extracting information from old documents is accurately identifying key information within images. One effective approach is using deep learning models that analyze document images to extract important information. This method has been among the most successful, yet it's important to note that providing annotated training data for these models can be a time-consuming and expensive process.

This paper presents an innovative approach that utilizes models trained on data from documents that have been converted into text-based formats. This approach is notable for being able to utilize a vast amount of publicly available information, thereby significantly reducing the need to manually label large amounts of visually complex data.
