This paper also presents experimental results that demonstrate several significant improvements, specifically: (1) achieving model accuracy on visually complex datasets that's comparable to state-of-the-levels; (2) achieving model accuracy of 84% on a newly created, challenging public dataset of 19th-century newspapers; and most importantly, (3) showing that models developed using this approach can be seamlessly fine-tuned into visually complex data with remarkable efficiency, specifically requiring 10 times fewer training samples and 10 times fewer training samples  times fewer manual labels to reach the same level of accuracy models that are trained on visually complex data.

The collaborations LIGO-Virgo and KAGRA have discovered merging compact binaries that generate gravitational waves, which offer profound insights into the properties of neutron stars and the population of black holes. This paper introduces neural network-based models to automatically classify the identities of the compact objects in binary mergers. The novel approaches, including one using only amplitude ratio data ratio at specific phases, demonstrate high accuracy rates, but slightly lower than optimal, in distinguishing between neutron star and black hole mergers when simulating data with minimal noise.

Our proposed framework, Application-Specific Enabler for Marker-based Neural Networks (ASE-MENNE), utilizes a unique approach to accurately predict social determinants of health in electronic health records. As social determinants significantly influence health status and are increasingly integrated into clinical data, there is a growing need for sophisticated natural language processing models with a deep understanding of context and nuanced information. Building upon a cross-attention mechanism, our ASE-MENNE framework identifies key social determinants and effectively fuses them with medical history for enhanced model performance. Experimental results on real-world data demonstrate the superiority of our framework over current baselines, resulting in substantial improvements in model accuracy. Furthermore, as a flexible and adaptable system, ASE-MENNE holds the potential for broader application in various NLP tasks within clinical data.

This work delves into the optimal motion of a scallop in a viscous fluid, influenced by its capacity to alter its shape at will, in line with previous research by Power (1972a,b). The study is highly susceptible to the cost of shape changes, leading to significant optimal movements when the cost is low and local solutions when the cost is high. Several optimal scenarios are examined and illustrated through detailed examples, some with no analytical resolution requiring efficient numerical methods for their study.

The COVID-19 pandemic significantly affected face-to-face meeting patterns in cities across 50 major US urban areas between 2020 and 2021. By leveraging mobile device data and a night-time illumination metric as a reference point for face-to-face meeting diversity, this study found that nighttime diversity decreased by about 10% on average during the pandemic. Nighttime diversity also varied greatly across different cities, times, and nights. Analysis of mobile data revealed that people's face-to-face meeting diversity declined during the pandemic, particularly in less diverse areas, at nighttime hours, and in urban neighborhoods. It also showed that face-to-face meeting diversity behaved similarly to nighttime illumination levels. Further research identified urbanization level, time of day, and nighttime temperature as key factors that influenced diversity. Behavior-altering policies had a greater diversity-reducing effect during the pandemic in areas with lower urbanization levels, at different times, and on warmer nights.

A new theoretical model is proposed to explain how massive protostellar clouds form and grow. The model incorporates three key factors: gas accretion massifying the protostar rapidly, which causes it to shatter and emit light, and the accumulation of interstellar clouds that may merge with the primary cloud, fueling further growth and expansion of the star-forming region. According to the model, there must be an odd-numbered "episode" of cloud accumulation and shattering to create a massive cluster, and it is predicted that there must be at least three such episodes to explain the existence of massive, centrally located stars in such clusters. Furthermore, clues to these episodes may be found by studying the water lines and other features in the spectra of individual stars and by predicting specific characteristics about the stars' masses and spins. The model is predicted to be testable and may provide insight into the behavior of water lines and other features in the spectra of individual stars.

For a mass-gap wedge-local QFT in two-dimensional spacetime, we've developed a method to directly attach a net of observables in a given wedge to a pair of modules within the same category of endomorphisms, using a natural equivalence. This connection establishes a bijection between unitary, wedge-local sectors inside the given net and the 'superselection sectors' corresponding to the endomorphisms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the category of sectors for the given net is a C*-rigid extension of the category of modules for a specific 2-category, 'endomorphisms', defined by the natural endomorphisms derived from the given natural transformations.

The potential adverse effects of excessive electromagnetic field (EMF) exposure on children and teenagers in educational facilities and medical institutions is a major concern.  This study focuses particularly on the high-frequency EMFs emitted from 5G cellular towers with an aim of assessing the potential risks on children and teenagers in various settings, including schools and hospitals, due to prolonged exposure. To gather necessary data, a computational model is used to calculate 5G tower exposure levels at near-field and far-field distances, using a combination of analytical and empirical methods. It uses a uniform linear array emulating 66 antennas to accurately measure the power density emitted at 3.5 GHz, and this method is applied to evaluate exposure in various scenarios, including real-world hospitals and schools in Pennsylvania, USA. Analysis of data shows that in most cases, exposure levels from 5G towers are below safety guidelines set by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection in both near and far fields.  However, there are isolated instances of elevated exposure levels detected in close proximity to 5G towers in some hospitals, and it was observed that lower frequency 5G bands may pose greater exposure risks than their higher frequency counterparts. Overall findings suggest that the potential adverse effects of EMF exposure on children and teenagers in educational facilities and medical institutions, due to prolonged exposure from 5G towers, are minimal and unlikely to occur in most settings, including those with multiple 5G towers in close proximity.

This research investigates a two-dimensional water domain affected by gravity, where the fluid flow includes a constant circulatory current, and the absence of wind forces, we prove that the Dysthe equation, modified to account for circulation and constant vorticity, accurately models the non-linear water surface dynamics under specific conditions for varying vorticity values. However, for wave patterns characterized by odd symmetry, identified by integer $\kappa$, the Dysthe equation with $\kappa$ set to 1 is found to be inaccurate, as it predicts unbounded amplitude growth over time, indicating the equation's failure in describing such wave patterns. In contrast, for these specific odd symmetry cases, we develop and apply a novel Hamiltonian water wave approximation, yielding accurate descriptions of long-term wave dynamics, and confirm this accuracy through extended numerical simulations.

This work introduces a novel approach to constructing differential shapes in a local convex topological vector space and demonstrates the validity of the Stokes formula. Our method builds upon the concept of locally convex multilinear maps to develop a multilinear path, serving as the foundation for defining differential forms and the exterior derivative. A key result is the proof of the Stokes formula for a combination of an exterior differential and the integration of differential forms over convex subspaces. This outcome has far-reaching implications, including the demonstration of the equality of exterior differential and differentiation with respect to a parameter under certain conditions. Our approach also aligns with the development of de Rham cohomology for convex sets, with additional references providing context and support.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments demands the independent generation of global and local paths by separate modules, each utilizing its own source of information. Although module independence provides the flexibility to utilize diverse information sources, the conflict between global and local objectives can result in suboptimal or oscillatory paths. A layering control strategy that seamlessly integrates local and global objectives has been successfully applied in various navigation scenarios and can be improved to incorporate diverse sensing modalities for robust local path generation. In this study, we present a method for integrating 2D sonar data with the layering approach to create an integrated navigation system for service robots. A case study on a library navigation task without visual feedback has been used to evaluate the system's performance, and the accompanying layering controller code has been made available for other researchers to utilize.

The prevalence of false news on social media has grown to become a significant problem, especially when it mimics real news. Research into detecting false news on social media is therefore crucial. One of the primary challenges in doing so is the lack of explicit indicators in false news articles. This research explores the potential of using text summarization techniques to distinguish false news from real news. The study employs both batch and sequential summarization models to generate abstracts of multi-sentence tweets associated with news posts. These generated summaries are then used as input features for machine learning classifiers to distinguish real news from fake. The results show that using high-quality summaries generated by sequential models in combination with a deep learning classifier yields the most accurate classification outcomes. This study ultimately aims to shed light on how the quality of text summaries can influence the ability to distinguish real news from false.

This research focuses on analyzing long-range interactions in $2$-dimensional Gaussian random fields, specifically examining the probability that the field remains positive within a given domain. Our study considers a Gaussian random field defined by a bending covariance and investigates the asymptotic behavior of the probability as the domain size increases. We derive the asymptotic growth rate for cases where the interaction range is finite and moderate, and our results for moderately long-range interactions build on existing work by Biskup, Frohlich, and Sen. In areas where no existing results apply, we establish the exponential growth rate for interactions that are moderately long-range.

Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) is an efficient and flexible technology for next-generation wireless networks, which has various applications in secure communications. In this paper, we explore the decoding patterns of nominal users in a power-domain NOMA system and develop a new technique to establish confidentiality. This technique enables a helper to facilitate secure transmissions between a source and a nominal destination by decoding its intended message and simultaneously sending another message from the helper to the destination. In a scenario without the helper, we analyze the decoding performance of nominal users and evaluate the security through information theoretic metrics. With the helper present, our technique's ability to protect transmissions is also analyzed. A stochastic geometry model is used to assess the feasibility of our security technique, considering a scenario where users are randomly distributed. Additionally, a new method is proposed to maximize the security capacity with the helper by adjusting the NOMA decoding boundaries.

An $k$-SPCA problem addresses a application-driven scenario in which a subset of data is organized into $k$ distinct sections, with the goal of identifying the most dominant component within each section. This paper presents an innovative approach to solving this problem by applying the principles of local search to a specific, under-explored variation of the problem that focuses on identifying multiple disjoint subspaces within data. The proposed method, Inertia-Local Search, leverages an inertial $\ell_1$-norm PCA algorithm to identify each separate cluster. Theoretically, the method is shown to converge rapidly to an optimal solution under specific conditions, with at least $k$-times the data required to achieve this convergence. The Inertia-Local Search algorithm has been put through a series of experiments to evaluate its performance in both artificial and real-world settings, with results demonstrating its efficiency in terms of both accuracy and processing time.

Erasmlv3 is an annotation dataset containing 14,877 questions with emotion intentions,
annotated using BERT for semantic accuracy. To engage the community in emulating the
annotation procedure and providing feedback on the current annotations' quality, we are
inviting you to:

- Examine the dataset to see if any emulations have been developed.
- Utilize BERT to identify and correct the errors in theemologic annotations.
- Provide a score that reflects the emologic annotations' quality.

The concept of stopping times is expanded to encompass totally ordered groups, and then used to examine 'energy contests' where a predator aims to deplete a prey's energy reserves within a defined time frame, taking into account the unpredictability of both actions and any external environmental factors. These calculations are supported by a jointly optimal control and stopping time model, and a Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs variational principle, leading to the existence of a solution through a dynamic programming approach.

Observing the ultra-soft spectrum of magnetic white dwarfs in asynchronous polars remains challenging, which is why studying these systems' X-ray properties is particularly valuable. Asynchronous polars exhibit a significantly lower X-ray emission rate compared to their asynchronous counterparts, our new analysis of the spectral energy distribution for four asynchronous polars, combined with comparisons to similar systems, supports this statistical trend. Moreover, we found that the X-ray emission rate in asynchronous polars is at least ten times lower than in normal polars, and at least a hundred times lower than in anomalous polars. We also found no difference in X-ray emission rates between normal and anomalous anomalous polars. These distinct X-ray emission rates may result from differences in the accretion patterns onto the white dwarf surface, affecting plasma heating processes.

This study presents two distinct approaches to solving the time-discrete Fourier-series-based fluid structure interaction problem for flexible shells: a monolithic segmented Reduced Basis Method and a monolithic coupled Reduced Basis Method. We develop a new algorithm for the former, which calculates separate basis sets for the fluid and shell fluids and couples them at the structure's degrees of freedom. Numerical experiments are carried out to compare the performance of both methods.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate independently, autonomous navigation systems are necessary. In this study, we present HiTMap, an autonomous navigation framework based on graph representation, capable of guiding a mobile robot through an unexplored environment. Initially, the robot maps its surroundings and divides the environment into modular segments during the exploration process. As it advances, it creates interconnected nodes representing each segment, thus generating a hierarchical graph that depicts the entire environment. To locate the most optimal path to a target destination, we employ the A* algorithm in conjunction with topological measurements on the graph. Our system demonstrates effective navigation in various ununexplored environments in simulation, and our framework is open-source, available on GitHub.

This paper presents a machine learning approach for detecting aggressive language on social media, specifically for the SEMEVAL-2019 Task 6 challenge. Our system achieved a macro F1 score of 0.625, placing eighth out of 43 participating teams. We developed two versions of classifiers: one where labels were assigned to entire tweets and another where tweets were segmented into sentences and labeled individually. The final decision on each tweet's label was made based on the most frequent label among its sentences. Our experiments used the provided training dataset along with an additional corpus collected from Twitter to pre-process characters in the 2019 test samples. Features included original Unicode characters and a range of contextual and graphological features. These features were fed to both traditional machine learning models like Logistic Regression and Linear SVM, as well as a BERT model adapted for three-way classification. The best performing model was an ensemble of classifiers with different features, evaluated using SVMs.

This research employs a two-axis resonator (TAR) composed of superconducting materials to take advantage of the Meissner effect for enhanced sensitivity in detecting local magnetic field changes through atomic interferometry. By leveraging the property of superconductors that expels magnetic fields, even minute variations can be detected as changes in the flux passing through the TAR. We theoretically analyze how a TAR's sensitivity is affected by the masses of test masses and the orientation of spins, atomic precession frequencies, and the magnitude of detected magnetic field variations. Calculations based on Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and rate-of-change considerations in superconducting materials lead to an optimal calculation of sensitivity, constrained by the TAR's relaxation time. Notably, proposed TAR designs with specific dimensions and materials can achieve extraordinary sensitivity, with sensitivity to magnetic field variation reaching as low as $10^{-19}$ rad$/\sqrt{Hz}$ at a 1-s integration time.

A novel effect, which we call the proximity-induced spin-polarized magnetothermal effect, arises from the combination of thermal gradients, magnetic field gradients, and strong spin-orbit coupling at interfaces between a transition metal dichalcogenide and a ferromagnet. Due to the spin-orbit coupling, a thermal gradient induces a polarization of spins perpendicular to the plane, making it possible to detect the resulting electric field through the anomalous Hall effect. Calculations using first-principles methods reveal the effect in various transition metal dichalcogenide/ferromagnet systems, with strong dependence on the specific materials used and particularly on whether there is a type I or type II band structure in the transition metal dichalcogenide. The effect offers a novel approach to manipulate the spin-polarized Hall effect using thermal methods, with implications for the development of spin-polarized sensors and thermal polarization devices.

The behavior of electrons near interfaces that are significant, particularly in structures with small gaps between metal layers for enhancing sensors or spectroscopy, needs to be considered, particularly the spill-out effect and nonlocality which often are disregarded. A theoretical model based on the random phase approximation is used to examine electron density changes and their impact on gap-plasmon modes in structures consisting of two metal layers. The calculations performed show that ignoring the nonlocality and spill-out effects results in an incorrect electron density distribution and a shift in resonant frequencies of low-gap modes, particularly in gaps smaller than five nanometers.

In the context of type theory, specifically the Calculus of Constructions, the presence of proof irrelevance and uniqueness of scalar replacement principles poses a challenge in achieving robust normalization due to their inability to be handled transparently. To facilitate various applications, particularly in computer-verified mathematics, multiple strategies have been developed for defining operations that facilitate the functional use of these features. Notably, work by Norrington and Urban demonstrates that certain transparent treatments are feasible with additional assumptions regarding the syntactic structure of terms. This research builds upon these approaches by introducing a transparent treatment of elimination forms for all inductive types, extending beyond product types, which is achieved through a combination of de Bruijn's technique and the split-context method. This new method is characterized by preserving the normal form of terms and is implementable using de Bruijn's linear order-based representation system.

This article serves as an introductory explanation of Topological SSH Model concepts, aimed at physicists and mathematicians/math students who may be unfamiliar with quantum physics. Although the content can be accessed without prior knowledge of the SSH model, topological insulators, or the Bloch bands, we have also included a section on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model's topological phase transition non-perturbative breakdown topological mid-band localized zero-mode within the context of adding an impurity.

In this paper, we provide an original perspective on finite Gaussian and finite elliptical mixture models, utilizing concepts from stochastic geometry and measure theory, particularly the Choquet theorem. Based on these foundational elements, our analysis leads to straightforward derivations of crucial properties and parameter estimates for these types of statistical models.

On the two-loop level, we've computed the QFT on AdS$_5$ vacuum amplitude, confirming the previously proposed on-AdS$_5$ data by Karateev, Zarembo, and Zarembo. Building on our method, a two-loop on-AdS$_5$ vacuum amplitude calculation with multiple graviton insertions has been performed. Additionally, we've derived the on-AdS$_5$ data for a scalar in the four-plug case and compared it to a direct two-loop amplitude computation, confirming consistency.

High-performance computing on object-based programming requires efficient memory management, particularly on GPUs, due to limited global memory and lack of pointer semantics. Developers often sacrifice performance for simplicity by using dynamically allocated memory, which can lead to suboptimal program performance. This paper introduces a novel memory allocation framework called DynaSOAr, a parallel stack allocator that maintains high program simplicity while delivering optimal performance through pointer translation. The algorithm allows dynamic memory allocation while minimizing data serialization/deserialization, and was implemented on a high-performance computing cluster running on object-based programming libraries. Benchmarking and case studies showed that DynaSOAr outperforms dynamic memory allocation in both iterative and data analytic applications on GPUs, with significant performance gains, and can be integrated with popular scientific data structures and object-based programming libraries.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a broad category of operators along with their commutators from generalized mixed Morrey space $ \rho_1(\tau_1, \tau_2, \phi) $ to $ \rho_2(\tau_3, \tau_4, \psi) $. Additionally, the article establishes the boundedness criteria for these operators and commutators under specific conditions, and derives a particular boundedness condition for Duzterer's operator and its commutator.

To accurately capture the relativistic effects in the study of magnetic atoms and their interactions on superconducting surfaces, a relative spin-orbit coupling within density functional theory is essential. Utilizing a self-consistent approach that incorporates spin-orbit coupling in both frozen-atom and supercell calculations enables the development of reliable models for describing Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. A comprehensive analysis of 1 Mn adatom and 1 dimer or trimer clusters situated on the Nb(110) surface was conducted to demonstrate the essential components for a precise and efficient description of QS states. A simplified model Hamiltonian can effectively reproduce the key characteristics of these states, yet including three-body interactions is necessary when examining multi-atom configurations. Notably, including relativistic effects in calculations has a substantial influence on the energy and electronic structure of magnetic atoms located on superconducting surfaces, which should be considered in any analysis.

Our proposed FourierMask presents a significant improvement over traditional instance segmentation methods by eliminating the need for explicit coordinate encoding in implicit neural representations. We achieve this performance gain through a transformation of the representation into four-dimensional space using Fourier mapping. We further refine FourierMask by incorporating two key adaptations: training it in three dimensions using a two-dimensional Fourier mapping and ensuring it outputs binary values. We evaluated FourierMask on popular datasets including ShapeNet, ModelNet, and CAD. The experimental results demonstrate that FourierMask outperforms current state-of-the-art implicit instance segmentation methods and outperforms the recent best approach on two out of three tested datasets.

This paper proves that for any function 'f' defined on a one-dimensional domain, there exists a two-dimensional domain 'D' where 'f' can be immersed without self-interactions. Furthermore, the document proves two key theorems: (1) a significant improvement to a previous finding by demonstrating the optimal bound of a specific class of functions 'f' defined by a finite-dimensional property, and providing a corresponding two-dimensional domain 'D'; and (2) a distinction from a previous result by showing that a specific class of functions 'f' cannot be expressed as a composition of monotone functions but can be expressed as the composition of two functions with specific bending characteristics, along with a specific representation involving a three-to-one function.

Current satellite-derived cloud retrievals rely on optical depth, a metric that fails to capture comprehensive 3D cloud structure. As clouds increase in opacity, photons traverse progressively thicker cloud sections along different retrieval paths, offering potential insights into cloud internal stratification. By analyzing previously retrieved data from the MISR and MODIS missions, we discovered that relatively narrow-swath sensors like MODIS are limited to observing the cloud's outer layers, characterized by consistent temperatures and pressures. In contrast, wider-swath sensors like MISR can probe deeper into convective clouds and locates a distinct core with unique pressure and temperature profiles. However, as clouds become more transparent, optical depth can no longer differentiate distinct cloud sections with differing pressures and temperatures. Our research suggests adopting advanced 3D cloud variable retrievals to better understand cloud physics and reduce atmospheric component estimation uncertainties in climate modeling.

This research focuses on analyzing the relationship between the duration of a laser pulse with a chirped profile and the ability of a plasma foil to induce and release transparency in relation to specific frequency points. By studying this transparency, we examined how negative electron layers form and the resulting forces on those layers, and discovered that reducing the pulse duration of the transparency point results in more significant electron displacement and residual current. Theoretical calculations and simulations indicate that shorter transparency-point-achieved-chirped pulses can result in higher ion acceleration. The optimal pulse duration for this effect is around 100 femtoseconds, leading to a 1.5 times improvement in ion energy when using such pulses in comparison to conventional unwrapped pulses.

The NASA Transiting Exoplanet Survey Telescope (TESS) has added to the planet discovery efforts led by the ground-based systems. With superior sensitivity to small planets and frequent observations, TESS significantly enhances the existing transit survey capabilities. In this study, we utilized the full potential of the TESS and Gemini observations along with data from the Literature, successfully identifying three new exoplanets, $Texo~b$, $c$, and $d$, within the TESS Optical Viewing Encyclopedia (TOVE) 712 system. The planets have distinct transit periods of 9.38, 16.50, and 26.30 days with enhanced signal-to-noise ratios, respectively. Notably, the host star exhibits a very low density of 3.05~$\rho_{\star}$, reminiscent of a very active young star with a magnetic field. Texo $b$ and $c$ both have masses below Neptune's mass and occupy the super-Eptune category, whereas Texo $d$ has a habitable zone transit and its mass remains unconstrained. This planet deserves closer examination with follow-up observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The TESS and literature data have contributed to our broader understanding of the vast population of small planets with transit characteristics and the potential for terrestrial exoplanets to also exist.

This paper presents a comprehensive examination of carbon and nitrogen substitutional doping in TiO2, with a focus on its electronic and magnetic properties. Using the rutile TiO2 as a model, first-principles calculations were performed to explore the stability and characteristics of various charge states. TiO2-C/N was selected for further analysis due to its stability across most charge states. Findings reveal that 11/12  and 11/12 frameworks are stable for  TiO2-C  and TiO2-N, respectively, showing similar charge distribution patterns in their neutral charge configurations. In addition, unpaired spins are concentrated on carbon or nitrogen atoms for -1 charge states, contributing to the magnetic properties of these frameworks. The -1 charge states of TiO2-C/N exhibit localized defect states within the band gap, which could influence its potential use in photocatalytic applications. Notably, TiO2-N with a neutral charge shows metastable localized defect states within the band gap, which could be a key factor in its ability to enhance the photocatalytic activity of TiO2. Overall, this study provides a detailed understanding of the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen doped TiO2 and its potential applications in future technological advancements.

The observation of new, exotic particles at colliders like the LHC has historically been facilitated by distinct signatures and elevated mass scales, often beyond the standard model. One significant challenge in this search is the overwhelming background noise from standard model particles that share similar characteristics. To overcome this obstacle in the top-quark sector, the concept of "Elastic Energy" has been put forth as a method to detect the production of elastic quarks. This detection can be achieved by measuring the transverse missing energy and summing the masses of jets in the final state. A preliminary estimation indicates that a particular model of proton-elastic collisions, where a heavy scalar decays into two top quarks, could be detected at the LHC with an 8 TeCMC, 100 fb^-1 dataset.

The method of measuring the intra-cluster medium's turbulence through the extraction of radial structure functions from spherical thermal X-ray emission profiles faces limitations imposed by profile extraction itself. This process inherently introduces ambiguities and systematic biases, which, if unaddressed, could distort the extracted radial functions and render comparisons with non-radial, turbulent datasets meaningless. Moreover, varying extraction radii might yield conflicting results regarding the presence of turbulence. For a thorough assessment of RFIT's ability to quantify intra-cluster turbulence, these issues must be resolved. This paper analyzes the impact of systematic errors on the structure function extraction and identifies radii of interest where reliable structure function values can be obtained. The effects of unmodeled temperature variations and spatially correlated measurement errors are modeled and calculated for observed X-ray clusters using the VCE algorithm. The results for VCE's bias are summarized in Figure 17, Figure 18, and Table 5, while the impact of intrinsic thermal fluctuations on structure function extraction is explored for a range of signal-to-noise ratios. The optimal radii for reliable structure function extraction are found to be between 0.15-0.25 $R_{500}$ for all scenarios considered. The most significant systematic bias (around 0.15 kK) occurs when thermal fluctuations are uncorrelated, which renders the radial structure function dF/dR over $R_{500}$ appear deceptively flat, thus supporting the findings of Bullock

In 1993, Erdos and Western posed an open query about the Ramsey property of richly colored infinite graph properties. The current paper takes steps to address this question by focusing on infinite graph factors. A calculated lower bound for the chromatic number of infinite graph factors is determined as 56 through the application of combinatorial methods. Specifically, it is shown that any infinite graph with a specific factor can be covered by 56 color classes, whereas the exact chromatic number may potentially reach up to 876 color classes.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way's bulge, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) spans 300 parsecs and is characterized by extensive, anisotropically shaped gas clouds with higher densities along their length. This paper builds on a hypothesis that the CMZ's anisotropy can be explained by elongated, rod-like structures densely packed within the region. Using 2D sub-millimeter observations of the APEX Legacy Survey of the CMZ, the study calculates the two-point correlation length in different directional orientations to provide evidence for this anisotropic framework. The results show a significant anisotropic pattern in the correlation lengths, corroborating the anisotropic density distribution and supporting the proposed framework. This anisotropic structure in the CMZ may also have implications for gas dynamics and the behavior of supermassive black holes in the region's center.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying Bell's Palsy by analyzing a person's eye movements in video content. Despite the availability of specialized datasets, real-world applications often encounter lower video quality and a variety of frame rates, which can hinder existing models. To tackle these challenges, we focus on collecting relevant features from eye-centered video data and training a robust classifier capable of operating across different frame rates. By conducting comprehensive evaluations across multiple datasets with varying quality, we demonstrate the reliability of our approach. Furthermore, we provide recommendations for future research in this area.

Our analysis focuses on the scalar quantum electrodynamics in four-dimensional spacetime, a widely used test case for quantum simulations, and in particular examines an integral for the photon production amplitude. We discovered significant differences between results obtained through variation and bi-local approaches to this amplitude. By investigating these discrepancies in the context of the full scattering probability, we attributed the differences to noise-related data contamination introduced by measurement errors. Furthermore, theoretical derivation revealed that the contamination could be minimized by mathematical operations that could be implemented experimentally. Notably, the proposed procedure's applicability extends beyond the specific example studied, having broader implications for interpreting corrupted data from qutrit-based measurements.

Researchers have introduced the concept of generating dense, spin-aligned positron-electron pairs via high-intensity laser interaction with metallic film coated with magnetic insulation. When these coated targets are subjected to intense irradiation, incoming photons stimulate a series of high-energy interactions with the electrons within the targets and the strong magnetic fields produced by the underlying magnetized layer. As a result, some of the generated positrons emit high-energy photons before escaping the targets, those which survive this process become spin-aligned due to their interaction with the strong magnetic fields and could potentially be assembled into dense positron piles. The feasibility of this approach is supported by theoretical modeling and experimental validation, with a viable target design proposed for implementation.

A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is considered wide if it is intersected significantly by conjugates of itself, resulting in a subgroup with a relatively large intersection index. As per our new finding, any finite group containing only wide subgroups is a semidirect product of a quasi-simple group with a modular group, where the subgroup being wide is denoted by $H$.

This paper presents a novel and power-efficient temperature sensing circuit, ideal for low-power applications, that minimizes the need for precise temperature calibration.  The proposed sensor is based on the thermal-mechanical expansion phenomenon, enabling it to generate accurate temperature readings without the need to adjust the conversion threshold.  The 0.5{\mu}m CMOS process used to create the sensor does not include P-type wells, making it suitable for a variety of fabrication processes.  The temperature detection circuit is connected to an external temperature sensor chip, and it successfully detected the temperature changes induced by the thermal-mechanical expansion phenomenon.  The experimental results indicate that the sensor can convert voltage to temperature with an inaccuracy of 1.4{\deg}C and a resolution of 0.24{\deg}C, and it can perform an entire conversion cycle over 1ms, as demonstrated in a 0.6V$-$1.8V supply range.  The entire design of the sensor is based on a 0.5{\mu}m CMOS process and includes only 0.65mm^2 of active area.  The proposed sensor is an ideal candidate for temperature calibration of thermal-infrared sensors and for reducing power consumption in devices equipped with multiple temperature sensors.

The study investigates the long-term stability of magnetic forces within stars that have magnetic fields aligned with the polar axis. Focusing on stars where magnetic field strength varies in the equatorial plane and remains constant along the polar axis, it confirms the existence of equilibrium configurations similar to those found in the Sun. However, numerical simulations reveal that small disturbances can significantly alter the magnetic field's intensity, ultimately disrupting the equilibrium and causing a star to transform into one with a different magnetic field pattern. This outcome occurs within approximately $10^5$ rotations, indicating a limit to the longevity of forces aligned with the polar axis. Consequently, it is hypothesized that magnetic fields within stars, such as the Sun, must be regenerated every $10^5$ years or less, likely through global convective processes responsible for the development of various global patterns, including those seen in solar spots and flares.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been an invaluable tool for studying complex fluids in multiple and disordered dimensions and can even apply to quantum field theories beyond perturbation theory. Despite the value of the FRG approach, its application can encounter difficulties due to the presence of an infinite number of relevant degrees of freedom within the flow. While the introduction of a momentum scale truncation facilitates the application of the FRG approach to continuous systems, it can lead to unphysical rapid flows in finite-dimensional models. This paper aims to apply and evaluate Frank's recent FRG formalism to the well-studied, smooth flow of finite-dimensional models, specifically the standard FRG flow of an $O(N)$ model in one dimension for $N$ values of 0, 1, and large $N$. By utilizing a new, well-defined flow equation, the authors contrast the results of the standard and new FRG approaches in the context of a simple scalar theory.

A music discovery and acquisition platform tailored to the immersive experience of the Meta Quest has been developed with the introduction of "Pied Piper." This innovative application addresses the music industry's primary concern of music discovery by utilizing a data-driven approach. The Pied Piper platform analyzes user listening habits and generates personalized recommendations based on the tracks they enjoy. In addition to recommending new tracks, the system also engages users through interactive features like music trivia and promotional discounts, effectively retaining users. The effectiveness of the recommendation system is supported by the use of neural network techniques, including implicit feedback modeling and genre-based prediction. A pilot project demonstrates the system's ability to generate accurate recommendations and retain user interest in music.

This working paper explores various structural elements within Lie groupoids and stacks formed from them, with a focus on deformations, vector fields, connections, and Connes' noncommutative differential calculus. It particularly examines the 1-Serre-Danies complex and its role in defining the Cheeger-Eilenberg cohomology of stacks.

A statistical analysis of 109 massive stellar progenitors, identified using continuum data, reveals distinct dynamical patterns in a gaseous core of the Dragon infrared dark cloud. Notably, 87 of these expanding outflows exhibit an average growth rate of $1.2 \times 10^{-6}$. This rapid core expansion poses challenges to the traditional idea of a self-regulated star formation process dependent on a static molecular cloud core, according to the infall model. Furthermore, a comparison of spectral energy distributions reveals characteristics of high accretion rates associated with massive stars, presenting challenges to a process that produces low masses. This suggests a potential pathway for the development of massive stars.

The characteristics of a potential star formation pathway, depicted in a diagram, exhibit characteristics of mixed systems, defined as having both high and low masses. However, evidence of massive stars awaiting birth, located in regions of high density within low masses areas, is presented as a potential example of an alternative star formation pathway.

The discovery of this new pathway challenges the conventional understanding of star formation processes and presents a potential model for the formation of massive stars located in regions typically associated with the development of lower mass stars.

Godel modal logics can be analyzed through the lens of modal-type dependencies within their algebraic and relational frameworks, extending beyond classical and intuitionistic modal logics to include many more complex systems. This approach enables the algebraic equivalent of a numerous Godel modal logic extensions to be determined efficiently.

The growth of LiDAR applications spans multiple industries, allowing for efficient and accurate data collection and analysis, often in hazardous environments. This technology enables LiDAR to create detailed 3D point clouds that depict target objects. Subsequent processing of these point clouds through advanced techniques such as feature extraction, object recognition, and scene analysis yields valuable insights into the 3D point clouds. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of LiDAR 3D point clouds, including their source, characteristics, and applications. It also explores pivotal stages in the machine intelligence process for 3D point clouds, including statistical analysis, preprocessing, preprocessing, feature extraction, point cloud classification, object detection, and segmentation. The paper further discusses current machine learning approaches and trends in this field.

The behavior of random fields evolving over time on geometric shapes has been extensively studied in various disciplines including probability theory, physics, and astronomy. We focus on a particular type of random field where spatial correlations remain unchanged over time, known as a stagnant random field. By examining this type of random field on the surface of a sphere, we look at specific functions that represent values within the field and examine when these functions reach extreme values at different locations. Traditionally, studies in this area have been limited to scenarios where the values of the function are determined by the positions within the sphere and a finite number of random variables. However, we expand on this by considering a more complex situation where the values of the function are determined by the locations within the sphere, an infinite collection of random variables that follow a specific pattern, and we identify the basic rules that ensure extreme values occur simultaneously at different locations under this more general condition. Moreover, we apply Monte Carlo simulations to a situation relevant to the detection of cosmic explosions known as binary mergers of neutron stars, and discover that using a more dense pattern of data transmission improves the consistency with which these events are detected.

The nature of the primary cosmic ray particles is determined by the detection of associated neutrinos produced when they interact with the atmosphere. While neutrino detectors like IceCube are capable of identifying such particles, their low numbers restrict the statistical analysis possible. The application of techniques from image processing to the study of cosmic ray and neutrino data allows us to investigate the direction of arrival associations between neutrino and cosmic ray particles over extended time periods and directional intervals. The analysis in this study uses IceCube High-Energy Start events and data from the IceCube and Pierre Auger collaborations to compare the direction of arrival associations of cosmic ray particles with neutrinos produced by cosmic ray interactions and those with external astrophysical neutrinos over 12 years of observation. The results show no statistically significant differences among the observed associations, and the study's sensitivity is sufficient to constrain possible extraterrestrial interventions or anomalous natural phenomena at a level of 0.17 parts per billion.

The flow of liquid foams is heavily influenced by their texture, and this in turn affects their friction properties. Through rigorous simulations combined with direct measurement, we establish a connection between the friction experienced by flowing foams and their internal structure. Notably, the friction coefficient in these foams follows a distinct non-linear relationship with the foam's texture, specifically its bubble size distribution. This finding indicates that the complex behavior of flowing foams can be described using a relatively simple framework, consisting of two interconnected variables: its friction coefficient and bubble coarsening process.

This paper introduces a comprehensive dataset containing 1,120 images across six categories of skin cancer, including actinic keratosis, melanoma, BCC, basal cell carcinoma, angioma, and nevus. Following initial classification attempts using both manual and automated methods, this study generated labels for the images. To analyze the dataset's balance, we calculated entropy and identified inaccurately labeled samples by combining outlier detection algorithms with unsupervised learning, specifically Local Outlier Factor. Ultimately, we extracted a more balanced subset of the dataset by removing samples that did not conform to their respective categories.

The behavior of fluid instability known as the Rayleigh-Taylor in a rotating frame of reference has been investigated, specifically how the rotation influences the shape and number of fingers formed. A setup was used to study this phenomenon where two immiscible fluids with varying densities are placed in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell that is also rotating. Notably, only the less dense upper fluid displays finger formation. It is observed that the rate of rotation first causes fingers to bend, then determines the number of fingers formed. Furthermore, only a certain number of fingers match the system's symmetry when subjected to rotational effects. A more complex relationship is found between the number of fingers and the rotation rate, which can potentially be described through non-dimensional parameters. It is concluded that increasing the rotation rate causes fingers to appear and then vanish, leading to a parameter region where a specific number of fingers, $4n$, is most prevalent. It is believed that this finding can aid in understanding the behavior of magnetic field generation processes.

Building on a novel concept, the Casimir function, we've developed a generalized canonical transformation that preserves the phase space volume for both Hamiltonian and non-Hamiltonian transformations. The transformation's conditions are clearly defined, and the benefits of this approach are discussed. The generalization of Liouville's Theorem is discussed, and the advantages of this approach in integrating non-Hamiltonian systems are highlighted. The success of this method is demonstrated through the free expansion of a gas, and potential applications in statistical mechanics are explored.

A cycle alkyne molecule, specifically isomer 2 of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (c-C5H5-C2H), has been detected for the first time in the interstellar medium using submillimeter spectroscopy, with a lower abundance limit of $1.4 \times 10^{-9}$ times that of HC3N.  Also detected are its structural isomer 1 and two ethynylnaphthalene molecules.  By analyzing these molecules through semi-rigid rotor simulations and accounting for their isomer-specific spectra, researchers were able to accurately measure the abundance of c-C5H5-C2H.  Its estimated lower abundance is $1.4 \times 10^{-9}$ times that of HC3N or $2.6 \times 10^{-12}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-2}$, with a detection significance of over three standard deviations.  Ethynyl cyclopentadiene's isomer ratio falls between $10^{-2}$ and 10 in this region, with a current ethynyl to phenyl ratio abiding by Heber's (2019) cycle alkyne inequalities.  The detection of these cycle alkynes supports the theory that these complex molecules can be formed through a photochemical process driven by external ultraviolet radiation acting on benzene and acetylene molecules within benzene-acetylene enclosures shielded from direct ultr

In Neural Machine Translation, current models often rely on local information, which can result in inaccurate probability estimations due to the "focus problem". To address this limitation, we introduce the Look-ahead Focus (LaF) model that allows the decoder to consider future information during the generation of each target token. By using self-attention with cues from previously generated tokens, LaF is capable of creating a core attention mechanism centered on a specific token for each step. The model's ability to organize its attention in a structured way is shown to lead to better performance, according to experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results indicate that LaF not only produces more accurate token probabilities but also leads to improvements in overall model performance, particularly on difficult cases. LaF's beneficial effects are observed across multiple dataset scenarios, with the model's structured attention mechanism showing significant gains in overall performance.

Computing professionals can't simply improve Gflops to boost performance, a limitation highlighted by Gordon Bell in 1997. Genuinely solving complex, real-world problems often demands extremely high computational power. A solution emerged from a group of scientists who decided to design a virtual computer with optimal features for collaboration, data management, problem solving, and efficiency. This concept, known as "The Grid," focused on gridware - a translation layer that adapts applications to the grid's constraints. Instead of focusing on improving raw computational power, the grid transformation aimed to improve cooperation, data handling, problem-solving, and efficiency. This approach has been implemented by leading organizations like CERN, but its full potential is often hindered by the need for extensive customization. A potential solution is offered by the Translation Layer framework, a modular framework that accelerates the development of gridware solutions by allowing for seamless integration of new features and functionalities.

In a unified dark matter-dark energy framework, researchers examined the impact of mutual dissipation between substance clusters on cosmic structure formation. They calculated the average energy loss for each cluster and incorporated it into the field equations, assuming that the dissipated energy converts to heat within each cluster. By studying the resulting model with equilibrium solutions, they derived an expression for the relaxation time. The model's parameters were then estimated by fitting them to observed data from four distant supernovae and the Planck's cosmic microwave background data. The fitted parameters led to the formation of stable density and scale factor cycles that match the observations. The model's Hubble parameter, growth rate of density fluctuations, and transfer function were compared to standard predictions, finding H and growth rate to be in agreement with observed data, though structure formation is suppressed. The model's predictions for the present values of equation of state, density fluctuation growth rate, and matter power spectrum were found to be consistent with observed data.

Understanding curiosity in young children is crucial for designing effective learning environments and activities in early childhood education. However, measuring curiosity in children within a natural school setting has remained an unaddressed gap in current research. This study introduces a novel method for measuring curiosity in children within a natural school environment, utilizing code-switched self-directed utterances and visual gaze patterns as indicators. Our findings suggest that the frequency of children observing objects without verbal expression, along with the use of metacognitive language in self-directed speech, can accurately predict curiosity levels within a natural school setting. This research implies that curiosity may vary within groups of children, and thus, it is essential to examine individual children's behavior to accurately gauge their curiosity. This study also highlights the potential of a newly developed multimodal approach to studying the complexity of children's learning processes within natural school settings, and opens up new avenues for using multimodal analysis to better understand children's learning processes.

Moving beyond a Gaussian covariance model called a Mat\'ern function to graphically correlated data offers a practical and flexible alternative. This modification visually represents pairwise data relationships, rather than relying on distance-based calculations. However, using a Gaussian covariance model has its limitations due to the requirement of positive definite precision matrices for all possible graph combinations. We present five alternative distributions that maintain the desirable properties of conditional independence and marginal normality, even under different graph configurations. Among these, three provide additional benefits of marginal precision matrices and closed-form marginal likelihoods - a crucial factor in evaluating candidate graphs. We discuss the properties of these alternatives, present estimation techniques for their parameters, and assess their performance through simulations. Ultimately, one of these distributions is found to be particularly effective, surpassing both the original Mat\'ern function and traditional Graphical Gaussian Models in terms of fit and predictive capabilities in various simulation scenarios.

The surge in size of modern metropolitan road networks makes it challenging for municipal officials to accurately track and manage traffic flow. Utilizing large fleets of ridesourcing vehicles and their trip data offers a practical solution to effectively monitor road networks. Although many studies have proposed methods for traffic estimation based on smaller fleets of taxis, these approaches fall short when applied to the larger urban road networks of today's major cities. This research aims to develop and evaluate detection strategies for complex road networks in cities with numerous intersections, based on fleets of ridesourcing vehicles. We formulated an optimization model for optimal sensor selection on urban road networks, focusing on maximizing overall observability. Given the computational complexities, we created and tested multiple algorithms to efficiently solve this problem. To accommodate the dynamic movements of vehicles, a linear programming model for traffic estimation was developed. Evaluations across various datasets from New York City, Los Angeles, and San Francisco revealed significant improvements in overall accuracy compared to existing methods. The results also showcased the capability of our proposed approaches to accurately detect complex urban road networks in large cities.

Neutrino and dark matter interactions with other particles are described by an effective field theory consisting of $J/\psi$ and neutrino/dark matter fields, and we've analyzed the constraints that $J/\psi$ decay into visible gamma rays and invisible particles place on these theories. Using decay rates and the visible final-state signature's cross-section for the neutrino case, as well as the $J/\psi$ width for the dark matter case, we derived the corresponding limits on neutrino and dark matter mass. We consider all possible final-state combinations of visible particles and investigate the relevant experimental data, including results from BEPCII experiments and the LHC. Our results are also visualized in the "neutrino chart" and we compare our effective field theory approach to traditional operator-based studies. Notable differences and the potential for effective field theory approach to provide more comprehensive and comparative insights are highlighted.

Recently, standard differential equations have gained significant attention due to their precise modeling of1T1-recognizable differences between two theories. As a result, analyzing these differences using sDSEs requires numerical methods to supplement the analytical solutions' limitations. Although several strategies exist for modifying Runge-Kutta methods to suit sDSEs, most are incompatible with sDSEs' dense output requirements. This study introduces the adaptation of the SDIMSA-RK method for sDSEs and presents a novel variable stepsize method incorporating this innovation. The new method's performance is demonstrated through several standard test problems.

Modern science and technology generate complex, multi-dimensional functional data sets. Analyzing such data sets can reveal hidden patterns and enhance functional data analysis techniques. This paper proposes a novel, original method called Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Analysis, or MUFSSA. This method involves transforming data into rotating components, making it comparable to its univariate counterpart, but with a unique approach to handling data in different dimensional domains. We examine the method's consistency and provide insights into its applications, including improving data accuracy, isolating influential functional data and extracting meaningful features. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, we look at its use in analyzing atmospheric data and predicting the onset of monsoons.

Recent studies suggest that self-supervised edge detection methods are prone to excessive stability and responsiveness, which could lead to facile performance on difficult differentiation tasks. Yet, the precise mechanism behind this phenomenon remains unclear, primarily due to a lack of study on more complex systems beyond simple neural networks with single edges. To address this gap and better understand the interplay between two types of decisions made by people and machines near the boundaries between categories, we investigate the dynamics of multi-agent cooperative systems situated at complex boundaries. We establish a theoretical basis for addressing such situations by drawing upon concepts from statistical physics and game theory. We then experimentally validate our findings through the investigation of a communicative two-agent system classified by two interconnected dynamical agents, which is comparable to real-world speech recognition systems tested across various domains. We identify the key factor contributing to both stability and reactivity performances: the alignment of two agents' communication signals. We also formulate the optimization problem to maximize the system's overall performance, which leads to counterintuitive but practical solutions to improve both performance simultaneously. We further test these solutions both theoretically and experimentally.

The Azéma–Yor time, a crucial element of the powerful Azéma–Yor decomposition, has long been the focus of extensive research. A key aspect of this time is its persistent behavior, observed in continuous stochastic processes such as Brownian motion. A notable property of the Azéma–Yor time for Brownian motion is its ability to eliminate unnecessary oscillations in the local time of the Brownian motion, resulting in global persistence. This paper extends the concept of global persistence to the study of random walks, specifically examining the behavior of their local times. We establish an analogous property of global persistence for random walks and prove that, with overwhelming probability, the Azéma–Yor time will only sample points where the local time is a record high. Additionally, an examination of a previously discussed phenomenon, known as the Azéma–Yor phenomenon, is included in this research.

Plasma sources are crucial components in plasma characterization facilities, used for recreating specific plasma conditions and testing plasma diagnostic techniques and methods.  However, the ability to control the plasma sources' output is limited, and often only one operating mode of the device is available.  At the IIsc Small Test Stand (ISHTAR) in the Indian Test Bed for Advanced Plasma Diagnostics, there is a need for additional control over the plasma produced by the sources.  Currently, the sources are operated in mismatched plasma conditions, and only a subset of their characterization is possible.  For example, a helicon plasma source, typically used in the mid-plasma region of the test bed, has been operated in its radio frequency (RF) driven mode, rather than its helicon mode.  In this study, an external matching network was designed and fabricated to allow for helicon mode operation of the source, and it was found that this allowed for a six-fold increase in plasma density at the mid-test bed region, from $1.04\times10^{10} m^{-3}$ to $6.44\times10^{10} m^{-3}$.  This increase in plasma density was also observed when using a linearly biased grid source, and it allowed for the demonstration of helicon mode operation of a medium-sized (115 eV, 6.44 x 10^10 m^-3) plasma and

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system of equations, ultimately leading to increased crop pesticide levels. A new set of state-dependent control measures is introduced to address this issue, before formulating an optimisation problem resolved via the Pontryagin principle. In addition, a mathematical principle is established to verify the derived necessary conditions for solution optimality, while potential applications of the model are illustrated through a numerical approach.

A histopathology image analysis task is complicated due to factors such as a vast disparity between foreground and background, a significant amount of noise, and a high level of detail.  To overcome these challenges, we present a nucleus identification model called W-Net, which is composed of two distinct parts: a convolutional neural network backbone that employs odd-numbered dilated convolutional layers to reduce the level of detail augmentation in order to effectively extract relevant features, and a novel hybrid decoding module that integrates a parallel connection of dilated convolutional layers and a precise correction module to precisely reconstruct the output, thereby effectively reversing the detail dimension alteration produced during the feature extraction phase.  Experiments conducted on two public datasets, PANDA and PTCres-01, demonstrate the superiority of our proposed W-Net model over the current state-of-the-art methods.

For a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $q$ being an odd power of $3$, we have achieved a critical advancement in understanding the local exchange theorem for odd special orthogonal and symplectic triples over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Specifically, we have established that for any two triples within the category of special orthogonal or symplectic types, there exists an infinite sequence of finite fields $\mathbb{F}_{q_0}, \mathbb{F}_{q_1}, \dots, \mathbb{F}_{q_i}, \dots$ (where $q_i$ is an odd power of $3$) such that for any given dimension $n$, the local exchange theorem holds true over $\mathbb{F}_{q_i}$ for all $i \geq n$. Our solution to this problem represents a significant improvement over previous methods, expanding the applicability of the local exchange theorem to include odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups, and doing so with a more manageable set of characteristics of the finite fields in comparison to earlier solutions.

Li and Shao previously obtained a prerequisite condition for a graph G to have its n-th repeated line graph G^(n) contain a hamiltonian path, where n is greater than or equal to 2. This requirement constitutes a index for G to be able to contain a hamiltonian path in its n-th repeated line graph. In this research, a condition is provided for a graph G to have its n-th repeated line graph G^(n) contain a hamiltonian path, based on cycle decomposition, which meets the theoretical framework established by Li and Shao. Additionally, several criteria are given for a graph G to have its n-th repeated line graph G^(n) contain a hamiltonian path, following edge and vertex transformations, which are examined in relation to the definition of a repeated line graph.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by swelling and membrane pore formation, can have both positive and negative effects during an inflammatory response that the immune system initiates. Although studies have already highlighted the role of pyroptosis in the progression of SARS-CoV-2 infection, there is currently no in-depth understanding of how pyroptosis affects the interaction between SARS-CoV-2 and the cellular membrane pores generated during the process. Furthermore, the impact of pyroptosis on the efficacy of drug treatments that target the inflammatory response has not been thoroughly investigated through quantitative analysis.

To shed light on these issues, we developed a single-cell mathematical model of pyroptotic cell death, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Utilizing this model, we analyzed the impact of membrane-pore induced cell death on cell survival, as well as the interplay between SARS-CoV-2 infection and subsequent pyroptosis, and the response to drug treatment in controlling the inflammatory response, and membrane pore induced cell death.

Our findings revealed that, in accordance with existing research, the cellular process of pyroptosis is induced by the SARS-CoV-2 protein main protease. In addition, we found that the membrane-pore inducing caspase-1 can also be activated by the viral protease, but the cell death induced by pyroptosis can be averted due to the rapid inhibition of infection.
